## 1. WHAT TWO MEN DID WITH ONE SHOVEL IN A ROOM OVER A ROOM

A man in his thirties was putting a window in the first floor of a building on a street off that parade and found a cement shovel standing on its blade in the middle of that room, holding itself up against a stack of plasterboard. He picked it up, walked it to the end wall, stood it against the boards on the same side of the door it had been on since November, and went on with his work. Twenty-five minutes later, at about ten past ten against a quarter to ten, the man in his forties came up an outside stair with a sheet of plasterboard under his arm, found the shovel standing in the door reveal, walked it about ten foot to the far end of the room and laid it flat on the top of that stack because he had both hands full, and never looked at it again. **He cleared his tools out of that room at about ten to twelve and has not been in that building since, and the man in his thirties cleared out at a quarter to ten and does not know the shovel moved, and it stands ten foot from where the first man set it and not one foot from where the second man set it down. Both of them saw a woman who works in a shop at the other end of that street that morning, ten foot apart across a counter, and neither of them said one word and neither of them has said one word since. The shovel is on that stack.**

## 2. WHAT A MAN BEHIND A COUNTER SAID, AND WHY IT WAS TRUE

The man in his forties went into a store at the bottom of a yard off a side street and found a sectional water tank with its board lid on and the water five inches down and four inches of sludge settled across the bottom of it and a float valve stuck wide open and running to waste through the overflow. He had been told at a counter on that parade, in about fifteen seconds, by a man who sells pipe and owns nothing, that nobody had had that lid off since before Christmas. The man in his forties acted on it the same morning, cleaned the tank out over two days in May, changed the valve and charged the man at the end of that terrace one hundred and ten pounds, and the sentence turned out to be true. **The man behind that counter could not have known it. It reached him from a man in a fleece, and from a man who used to keep keys to those yards, and from a man who had a look at that tank at Christmas, and not one of the four owns or has a key. The man in his forties has never asked where he heard it and the man behind that counter has not mentioned a tank since and would not remember saying it. The man in his thirties was at the gate of that yard about a minute on the second of May and went and did his own work.**

## 3. FOUR POSTS, AND WHAT A WOMAN BEHIND A COUNTER SAID ABOUT THEM

The man in his thirties spent one day in a yard off a street off that parade putting four galvanised posts up for a washing line, dug them, concreted them, and knocked the third one out and did it again because it leaned over a raft. A woman who lives in that house came out and asked whether the line would take a wet sheet, and got a straight answer about washing lines and wet sheets and was not asked for anything else and put no name to him. On the Monday before, the man in his forties had stood at the corner of that street with a trolley and seen a man with a bar and a shovel and a string line in a yard, and had said in a shop, in four seconds, that there was a man down the end of that street with four posts up. On the Friday, at about half past four, the woman who works in a shop put that back to him at her counter and he said neither yes nor no, and asked her nothing, and went out and put the line up. **Nobody has raised it since on either side, and the four posts are in that yard with a dead straight line on them and a coil that has not been out of its wrapper since March.**

## 4. A MARK IN THE BOTTOM OF A BAG, AND TWO MEN WHO LOOKED AT IT

An unnamed man was in a first-floor flat on that first of May for about ninety minutes, doing a length of pipe and a stopcock, and put his thumb into a hard dark place about the size of his two hands in the bottom of a canvas toolbag on a shelf, and said nothing about it to the man in his sixties who was in the room with him. **THE CHAPTER DOES NOT GIVE THAT MAN AN AGE AND NEITHER MAY THIS BLOCK.** In the same flat that afternoon the man in his forties asked to borrow a screwdriver, and the man in his sixties went to that shelf and opened that bag for the first time since he gave the trade up, and saw the same place from the inside, and looked at it for about four seconds, and did not touch it, and decided it was grease and a wet rag and a wood stove thirty inches away. He put the bag back with that place against the wall and said nothing then or since. **That man has not been back in that flat and will not, and the man in his sixties has not been in that room again, and the two of them will never mention a bag to each other. Deciding that a thing is nothing and being right about it are two different things and only one of them happened.**

## 5. WHAT A MAN IN HIS FORTIES TOOK OFF A SHELF, AND WHY NOBODY ASKED

The man in his forties went into the back room of the man in his sixties at about twenty past nine on the seventh of May to find a stop tap, on his own, with a key he has never asked for, and came out of that room with a thirteen-inch dovetail level in his bag off the shelf by the window, because he had a stair carriage to do the next morning and his own level was in a van in another town until the Wednesday. He took nothing else. At about half past four that afternoon the man in his sixties came into his own room and stood in the doorway, went out, came back, and stood in the doorway again, and looked at a pale rectangle about thirteen inch wide on the plaster where a level had been standing for about twenty-five years, and went downstairs and made his tea. **He has not asked the man in his forties, has not asked the man in his thirties, and has not stood in that doorway a third time. The level is in a van at the top of that town on a shelf above a wheelarch and will be there on the Wednesday, and what was in the bottom of that bag is not found out by anybody in this borough.**

## 6. TWO MEN AT OPPOSITE ENDS OF ONE RUN, AND A WOMAN BEHIND A SQUARE OF GLASS

Two men stripped seventy foot of cast iron heating pipe out of a workshop over two days and started at opposite ends and met at a cast-iron column in the middle of it on the second morning at ten past nine. The man in his thirties wanted the new pipe over the top of that column on a bend and could have put it there and had done it in a school once. The man in his forties had measured and the only way to carry it past that column was to fix the clips to the far face of it and take the round. They talked for about six minutes. The man in his forties did it his way. At about twenty past one on the second afternoon the man in his thirties took his own length out again in about ten minutes and they did the last nine foot together in an hour and a quarter without a word about it. The woman who works in a shop sat at a desk in a brick office at the near end of that workshop behind a square of wired glass in that door for the mornings of both days and saw all of it, and said nothing to either of them then or since. **They shook hands on that yard at five past five on the second day and got into their vans. Nobody has asked either of them how that job went, and she is not going to find out.**

## 7. WHAT A WOMAN PUT INTO A MAN'S HAND, AND WHERE HE LEFT IT

On the fifteenth of May, with six feet of conduit on the counter and no bags left, the woman who works in a shop put a green and white wire birdcage into the man's hands so that he would hold it while she measured. It weighs about four pounds, its door does not work, and nothing could ever be shut in it. He took it because his hands were there, and he put it in the back of his own van, and it rode on the floor behind the passenger seat for ten days and moved about four times a day and came out entirely for one job. The man in his thirties was ten foot off at that counter and asked one question about the door and got one answer and has not come back to it. On the twenty-fifth of May the man in his forties stood it on its base with its back against a brick pier under the hood of a gate at the bottom of a lane he was in once in February, because his arms were full and the light had gone, and drove off. **The woman has not been down that lane since March and does not know there is one. The yard belongs to a man who has not set foot in it since the middle of May and has no idea what is standing against his pier, and he was not there when it was put down. Neither of them will raise it and the cage is still there.**

## 8. FOUR FOOT OF MARBLE AND TWO REASONS THAT DO NOT MEET

A Victorian marble chimney piece in a crate, on a slate base, about four foot wide and about three hundred and twenty pounds, has been against the north wall of a store at the bottom of a turning off the Cleeve road since about 1990. The man in his forties has a key to that store and has been in it about four times a month for six years and has walked past it about thirty times and has not touched it, because in thirty years he has not taken a thing out of a locked room to put in his own van, and because it came out of a house, and because he has nobody to say the sentence to. The man in his thirties has been in that store twice and could have it out in a morning with a van and four blankets, and has not, because it would take two men to get down and a third on the boards and he has not got a second man and there is nobody in this borough he could ask and he does not intend to be the one to ask. **They passed each other twice that afternoon in that yard, and neither of them said anything about the marble, and neither of them will ever know what the other one's reason was.**

## 9. WHAT A HOT CUPBOARD DID TO A MAN, AND WHO NOTICED

The man in his forties spent about eight hours on a third-floor bathroom on the twenty-second of May and the isolation valve was in a hot cupboard off a dark half-landing, the size of a man, with a cylinder in it, and the door of it was off one hinge screw. He was in there twice with his head and his shoulder in. The first time he came out and was wrong for about a minute and went back and finished the valve. The second time, at about twenty past one, he came out backwards at about ten to two, got four steps down, sat on the bottom step of the upper flight in the dark with his bag between his feet and his hand across his eyes for about six minutes, and then finished that bathroom and left that flat at half past four. The man in his thirties went up that stair at about ten to two, saw him on that step, carried on up, said nothing, and has not mentioned it and is not going to. At about twenty to six the man in his forties put his hand flat on the counter of a shop for two seconds while he was being given his change, and the woman who works in a shop was on that counter and noticed and has not mentioned it. **Nobody rang anybody. The door of that hot cupboard is still standing two inch out from its frame and nobody has looked at the hinge.**

## 10. WHAT A BOROUGH DID ON THE TWENTY-EIGHTH OF MAY

About nine people were out on that parade on the Monday morning and most of them were on it for under ten minutes and not one of them was carrying anything for any of the other eight. In a room at the back of one of those shops a deal table that has rocked since before Christmas stopped rocking, because the woman who works in a shop put it to him across her counter at about eight that morning, in about five seconds and in no way out of the ordinary, while he was buying washers, and he agreed on the spot because the pipe happened to be out, and he gave it three quarters of an hour at the tap on the outside of that shop, and then at about a quarter to nine, on his way out, he got down onto the boards, put a three-foot length of batten under the short leg and knocked it home and cut it off square, and told nobody. The woman who works in a shop went into that room at about ten for a sheet of paper, put her hand on that table, found the batten, and did not go and get him. Four answers to one question are still going round and none of the four can be put next to any of the other three, and nobody has said what they are answers to, and nothing has come out of anybody in three weeks. A wire birdcage has been standing under the hood of a gate at the bottom of a lane since the Friday before, and the man that yard belongs to has not been down it since the middle of May. A clock in the hall at the bottom of that parade switches the light off at four and there was nobody in that building to see it happen. **The line under the last entry in a book in a block by the water stood empty that day for one thousand two hundred and seventy-nine days and nobody was in that room and nobody counted it, and the one thing nobody in that borough would be able to explain is the same one it was a fortnight ago.**

## 12A. THE VERBATIM-SPAN METHOD AS IT WAS BUILT FOR THIS BATCH, AND THE THING THAT WAS WRONG IN THE FIRST BUILDING

**ONE, THE THRESHOLD IS NINE TOKENS AND IT IS NAMED EVERY TIME. TWO, THE SCRIPT COMPARES TOKENS AND NOT CHARACTERS, ON `[a-z0-9']+` APPLIED TO LOWERCASED TEXT, AND A TOKEN THAT IS NOTHING BUT APOSTROPHE MARKS IS A QUOTATION MARK AND IS DROPPED. THREE, THE H1 TITLE LINE IS DROPPED, EVERY `---` LINE IS DROPPED, AND EVERY STANDALONE ALL-CAPS PARAGRAPH IS DROPPED, WITH OR WITHOUT BOLD MARKERS. FOUR, A SPAN IS A MAXIMAL RUN OF NINE CONSECUTIVE TOKENS SHARED WITH THE COMPARISON SET, EXTENDED BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON FROM EVERY REAL POSITION THE NINE-GRAM OCCUPIES IN THE SET FILE, AND NOT FROM THE HEAD OF THAT FILE. FIVE, EVERY SPAN IS ASSERTED CONTIGUOUS IN THE OTHER FILE BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON, AND THE ASSERTION IS IN THE SCRIPT AND NOT BY ADDING ONE N-GRAM HIT TO THE NEXT. SIX, A PARAGRAPH BOUNDARY IS A SENTINEL NO TOKEN CAN EQUAL, IN THE TARGET AND IN EVERY SET FILE, AND NO SPAN CROSSES ONE, WHICH IS IMPLEMENTED AS A TEST THAT NEITHER SIDE OF THE MATCH LEAVES THE PARAGRAPH IT STARTED IN AND NOT AS A TEST THAT THE TWO PARAGRAPH NUMBERS ARE EQUAL. ## 1. WHAT TWO MEN DECIDED ABOUT A TREE IN THE SAME WEEK

A westerly on the night of the twenty-seventh of May put about seven foot of a limb off a lime that stands on the boundary between two back gardens in a street off that parade, and it took a length of close-board off the fence and left it hanging. Both men in those gardens had a right to have it cut away. The man in his thirties decided on the Tuesday that he was not going to have it cut, and he said so out loud twice, once to the woman who lives in that house and once to the woman who works in a shop. The man in his forties came into the other garden on the Thursday through a way in that nobody keeps shut, for a measurement that had nothing to do with a tree, looked at the limb for about a minute, and put his tape back in his bag. **Neither of them knew the other had a right at all, neither of them has said one word about it since, and neither of them ever will, and the limb is still across that fence and the length of close-board is still off its nails.**

## 2. WHAT A MAN SAID HE HAD NOT GOT

A man in his thirties asked a man in his forties, at a counter in a shop off that parade on the first of June, whether he had got a pair of reading glasses he could borrow for an hour, having seen him use his own three weeks earlier to read a price list. The man in his forties said, in about four seconds, that he had not. **He has. They are in the middle pocket of a holdall in a bag on a hook in his own van, and they will be there on the Monday, and nobody anywhere has asked him for them since and nobody is going to. He will not lend a tool or a spanner or a tape to anybody either, and he hands the woman who works in a shop a pencil as soon as she asks for one, and the two of those facts sit a hundred yard apart in the same day and neither of them is said out loud. The day it cost him was the day he set a shopfront out from a drawing he could not read, and the job took an extra day and the head of it is not the head that drawing calls for, and nobody will ever know but him.**

## 3. WHAT A SHEET OF IRON LIFTED OFF A LEAN-TO, AND WHO PUT IT DOWN

A westerly on the first of June lifted the top sheet off a lean-to roof in a service yard and let two days of rain into a corner where a man keeps boards. The man in his forties was in that yard on the Monday because his own van has nowhere else to go, and he went up his own ladder and did the whole head of that roof properly, taking three more sheets off as well, and he told nobody and nobody knows. The woman who works in a shop found out at ten past ten and did not go and get him. **That roof will now hold a storm at the end the man in his forties was standing at. It will not hold one at the other end, where the concrete is higher than the head of the fall and has been since the lean-to was built in April, and there is an old damp mark five foot up a wall in that corner that was there in April and is there now, and she put her own hand on that wall in the April and said out loud that there was a wet mark on it. Nobody has ever joined the two halves and nobody is going to.**

## 4. A CRACKED PANE ON A STAIR, AND WHAT THREE PEOPLE DID ABOUT IT

The opening light of a casement on a first landing in a block of eight flats was cracked from a corner in April and somebody had put two strips of tape over it. The man in his thirties went up that stair in May for a cistern and left it, and the man in his forties went up four steps above a passage in June for a delivery and left it, and neither of them will ever know what the other one made of it. The woman who works in a shop was in that block in June with a bolt in a bag and no better place to put it, and she stood on the step and looked at that window for about a minute, and then she went and did nothing about it for a week. Then she did it. **She took the pane out on a Saturday with cardboard on the stair, had it cut for nine pounds on her own account, bedded it in on a second Saturday, and came back a third Saturday to touch up a crescent of chalky paint on the sill. Nobody there asked her, nobody there saw her, and nobody there knows, and, at midsummer, a man from the uppermost flat came down for his post, looked at a window, and went back up.**

## 5. A WINDOW CARRIED TO THE BOTTOM OF A LANE

The man in his forties took a sash window out of a room in an empty house at the top of a lane in June, when his own van was eight miles off until two o'clock, and carried it about a hundred and twenty yard down that lane on his shoulder and stood it on its edge against a wall on the grass at the bottom, face in, with a piece of broken putty on the bottom of the frame. **He had never once been to the bottom of that lane in six years, and he went because he wanted to know whether the made ground at the head of it would take a loaded lorry for a block delivery on the Thursday, and he got the answer by putting his boot in it and putting a mark on a gate post in chalk, and the window has nothing whatever to do with the ground. The man in his thirties was in a gateway thirty yard behind him and offered to take the near end and was told he was all right, and has not thought about it since and does not know what it was. It is still on that grass and it will be there in the cold.**

## 6. WHAT TWO MEN LEARNED ABOUT EACH OTHER IN ONE HOUR, AND DID NOTHING

On the morning of the sixteenth of June a man behind a counter in a shop off that parade told a man in his forties, to his back, that a man in his thirties had bought a set of tools off him, which is true, and which means the man in his thirties has stopped hiring and is setting himself up. The woman who works in a shop told the man in his thirties, across her own counter the same morning, that the man in his forties has a yard past the junction, three men in it, pays all three, and puts his own name on every job that leaves it, which is also true. **Neither man turned round. Neither man asked. A third of an hour later the two of them took the two ends of a length of board off a high rack in that shop and put it down on the other rack in about four seconds without a word, and then each of them left by a different road, and neither of them has ever put either fact to anybody.**

## 7. A GATE, AND A MAN WHO IS NOT COMING BACK

A gate on a back yard behind a short terrace had been dropping since February, dragging on the flags, with the bottom of its hinge stile gone soft. The man in his forties went into that yard on the Wednesday of the twentieth of June through a gap where a gate does not shut, for a measurement, and lifted it, and then cut the soft wood out, let in two new lengths of oak, set new hooks in the pier, cut a new keeper and hung it so it closes without being tight. **He was there about three quarters of an hour and nobody saw him and nobody asked. The man in his thirties was in that kitchen all day, came out with a cup in his hand, saw the new keeper, told the man in his sixties at four that afternoon that the gate was all right now, and was told that the man he was talking about was not in the house. The man in his sixties went out at ten past four, found it shut and latched, pushed it and it swung and came back, and did not look at anything on it, and has not asked. The gate was hung on the same hook with the same screw in the second week of January by one of four men emptying that house for a death, and he was one of those four, and he put it back up in four minutes because it was in the way, and he has not been near that yard since and does not know whether it is shut.**

## 8. A DOOR, TWICE, AND THE ONLY PERSON WHO SAW IT BOTH TIMES

The front door of a shop off that parade has had nothing holding it back under it since about March, and there is a folded strip of stiff paper wedged under it, and in a westerly the door stands out past a hundred degrees and then comes back further than it went out. **It caught the man in his forties on the shoulder at half past ten on the twenty-fifth of June as he went out with a bag, and he stopped it with his hand and walked away. Four hours later it caught her on the outside of the forearm above the wrist as she went out backwards with ten foot of conduit in her arms, and she stood against the front of that shop for about two minutes with one hand over her arm while the parade went past. The man in his thirties saw the first of those and then saw the second, and he is the only person in this borough who has watched that door do it twice, and he said nothing then and has said nothing since. She said nothing to the man in his forties at five that evening and he said nothing to her, and a fortnight on neither of them has raised it, and the paper is still under that door.**

## 9. A WALL STARTED IN JUNE AND FINISHED IN JULY, AND A MAN WHO CAME DOWN THE STAIR

The man in his sixties took the paper off the long wall of his own front room on the eighth of June and filled about nine foot of it and stopped at the corner by the chimney breast, and has not touched it since. On the Saturday after, the man in his thirties came down that stair for a length of pipe, found the room open and the light on, and took two square yards of that fill off the wall in four pieces because it had gone off in blisters. **He came back on three evenings in that month, wetted the old plaster at night and again in the morning, redid the blown patch by the fireplace first, cut the arris off the chimney side and got that corner right first time, and did exactly the twelve foot of that wall and nothing else in that room, and he carried his own bucket and his own boards out every night and did not touch one thing that was in it. At ten past seven on the evening of the fourth of July, the man in his forties, who has carried a key to that passage door for six years and has never been asked for it, came through it with a ladder over his shoulder and saw a man working through an open door, and neither of them said a word, and the man in his forties went back out. On the Sunday, at half past ten, the man in his sixties came in, looked at the finished wall for about ten seconds from the doorway, put the light off and went and made his tea. The trowel is still on the ledge of that bay and the bag of plaster is still in the corner with the top folded over.**

## 10. WHAT A BOROUGH DID ON THE SIXTH OF JULY

That parade went through the whole day. The man who puts shutters up was down it at twenty past six and was going back up it at half past seven, and a bicycle belonging to a man who works eight miles off was lying across a footway outside a shop on that parade, and he put his steps down, stood the bicycle against that wall four foot further in, picked his steps up and went on, and nobody on that parade early on the Friday morning saw it. The woman who works in a shop was in a room at the back of her own shop with a bench in it and no table, the light off and her coat on, and missed all of it. She opened at ten and she was on her feet until about half past six, and she went into that room twice more and it was as she had left it both times. About nine people were on that parade over the day and none of them was doing anything for any of the others. The hall at the bottom of that parade is on a meter, was shut, and put its own lights out at four with nobody in the building. **Four answers to one question are still going round this borough, one of them is in more mouths than the other three, there is no fifth, none of the four can be laid against any other, nobody has said what they are answers to, and the question is still a question. One woman in this borough has ever had the book in her hands. The line under the last of its nineteen entries stood open across one thousand three hundred and eighteen days and was not touched and nobody was in that room.**

## 12A. THE VERBATIM-SPAN METHOD AS IT WAS BUILT AND USED FOR THIS BATCH

**ONE, THE THRESHOLD IS NINE TOKENS AND IT IS NAMED EVERY TIME. TWO, THE SCRIPT COMPARES TOKENS AND NOT CHARACTERS, ON `[a-z0-9']+` APPLIED TO LOWERCASED TEXT, AND A TOKEN THAT IS NOTHING BUT APOSTROPHE MARKS IS A QUOTATION MARK AND IS DROPPED. THREE, THE H1 TITLE LINE IS DROPPED, EVERY `---` LINE IS DROPPED, AND EVERY STANDALONE ALL-CAPS PARAGRAPH IS DROPPED, WITH OR WITHOUT BOLD MARKERS. FOUR, A SPAN IS A MAXIMAL RUN OF NINE CONSECUTIVE TOKENS SHARED WITH THE COMPARISON SET, EXTENDED BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON FROM EVERY REAL POSITION THE NINE-GRAM OCCUPIES IN THE SET FILE. FIVE, EVERY SPAN IS ASSERTED CONTIGUOUS IN THE OTHER FILE BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON. SIX, A PARAGRAPH BOUNDARY IS A SENTINEL NO TOKEN CAN EQUAL, IN THE TARGET AND IN EVERY SET FILE, AND NO SPAN CROSSES ONE. SEVEN, A CHAPTER IS NEVER INCLUDED IN THE SET IT IS COMPARED AGAINST AND EACH FILE OF A SET IS COMPARED SEPARATELY. EIGHT, THREE CLASSES ARE EXCLUDED AND RECORDED AS A COUNT AND NOT CHASED: A DATELINE, A FIGURE'S OWN BY-NAME DESCRIPTION, AND A BOROUGH'S OWN RECURRING PLACE NOUN. NINE, THE CONTROL IS ASKED FOR BEFORE ANY FIGURE IS BELIEVED AND IS TWO PAIRS AND A PLANT. TEN, EVERY FIGURE IS TAKEN AGAIN AFTER EVERY REPAIR AND AGAIN AT THE END.**

**AND THE FIFTH DEFECT OF THE 0022 BUILD WAS CARRIED FORWARD AND NOT REINTRODUCED, AND THE ONE THING THAT WAS WORTH CHECKING WAS THE SIXTH, WHICH IS THE HEAD-NOUN SET. IT HOLDS FIGURES AND NOT PLACES, BECAUSE A BY-NAME DESCRIPTION DESCRIBES A PERSON. A SPAN IS A BY-NAME DESCRIPTION ONLY IF THE WHOLE SPAN SITS INSIDE A SINGLE NOUN PHRASE THAT OPENS WITH A DETERMINER AND THAT HEAD NOUN AND RUNS ON UNTIL THE FIRST TOKEN THAT IS NOT PART OF IT, AND A SPAN LONGER THAN THAT NOUN PHRASE IS PROSE AND IS REAL REUSE. WITHOUT THAT LENGTH TEST A PASS EXCLUDES A FINDING, WHICH IS THE SAME FAILURE AS A PASS THAT ADDS AN ENTRY TO A LIST, ONLY INVERTED, AND A PASS THAT EXCLUDES MORE THAN IT SHOULD HAS HIDDEN A FINDING. **

**AND THE SIXTH FINDING OF THIS CLASS IN THIS REPOSITORY, WHICH IS THE MOST PRODUCTIVE ONE YET, IS THAT THE ACCOUNT'S OWN FIGURE TAGS ARE THE THING THAT KEEPS FAILING THE LENGTH TEST, AND THE REPAIR FOR IT IS IN THE CHAPTER AND NOT IN A LIST OF EXCEPTIONS. A SPAN THAT OPENS ON A FIGURE'S OWN TAG AND RUNS ON PAST THE VERB IS NOT THE TAG AND IS A REUSE, AND IT WAS REPAIRED IN EVERY CASE BY SENDING THAT figure somewhere else in the sentence: a man in his thirties became a man, a man in his forties became the other one, a woman who works in a shop became she. **A PASS THAT ADDS AN ENTRY TO A LIST IS A PASS THAT HAS NOT FOUND A DEFECT.***

## 1. WHAT A WOMAN ASKED HIM, AND WHAT HE WAS TOLD SIX WEEKS LATER

She works behind a counter off that parade and he comes in most weeks for a box of something. On the seventh of July she asked him, without any weight on it, whether he had eaten properly in this town since Christmas, and he said no. She has not raised it since and does not know she said it. He did nothing with it for six weeks, told nobody, went on eating at half past one in his own van with the doors open, and did not go and see whether it was still true.

Six weeks on, beside an open van at the top of a street, a man in his sixties told him that the other one has had no telephone since the November before last and goes to the call box at the end of that street to ring. The man in his forties put that against six years of a number he has never used, and left the number where it was.

On the Saturday morning the two of them met going in opposite directions at a blind end where there is not room for two. One of them said good morning. The other raised a hand four inches and carried on. **Each of them is holding one true thing about the other and neither knows the other has anything.**

## 2. A STACK OF IRON, AND WHAT HE DID WITH AN HOUR

There is cast iron against a gable end on that parade that came off a roof in the summer of 2017. A man took it out of that roof, put it out at the kerb and asked a man in his forties whether he wanted any of it; the answer was no, and then a promise to come back next week, and the promise was the reason for the no. The iron has been there ever since.

On the tenth of July the man in his forties stopped in front of it at ten past two in the afternoon, put his hand on the top length, and stood for about ten minutes while a woman and a cyclist and a lorry went past. He worked out where the iron would go and who would take it and when, and he was right about all of it, and none of it was any use to him. He then sat in his own van with the engine off for half an hour. **He has told nobody, nobody has put anything to him, and the iron is where it has been since 2017.**

## 3. TWO MEN IN ONE BUILDING, AND THE ONE BELOW THEM

A man in his forties lay across three boards on a parapet and found them sound and left them where they were. Under his feet, a man in his thirties took a kitchen unit out of the top flat. At the bottom of the same building a man in his sixties watched a van, a pair of legs over a parapet, and a screwdriver land on the flags, and then drank his tea and did not go out. **The two men never knew the other was in that building. He has said nothing about any of it. The screwdriver is still on those flags.**

## 4. FIVE TIMES, AND NOBODY PUT ANY OF THEM RIGHT

There is an empty building at the top of a street. A man in his forties told a woman behind a counter on the sixteenth of July that he had never been inside it. He had stood in the yard behind it in April, on his own, with nothing said to anybody. Two men from a town eight miles off had already asked him the same question twice and he had answered both, and he wanted the answer on the record in his own mouth before either of them asked a third time.

He said it four more times over the next four weeks, once to a man in his sixties in a passage, and once at that counter to nobody at all. She believes him. Nobody in this borough has anything with which to correct her. **What was a sentence has become a fact about him, and he is not going to take it back.**

## 5. WHAT WENT INTO HIS HAND, AND WHERE IT IS

A box of mixed crockery came into that shop in June and everything in it went except one saucer with a chip through the rim. It sat on a sill behind that counter for six weeks. On the twentieth of July the woman put it into the hand of a man in his thirties that was hanging free because his other arm was full of dowel, said one word, and went back round the counter. He asked nothing.

He drove with it on the passenger seat and then, at about half past four that afternoon, put it into the offside door pocket on top of a folding rule. It has been there since. He has opened that pocket four times. **He has no idea why she gave it to him and has decided nothing about it.**

## 6. THIRTY FOOT OFF A HOOK

A man in his forties crossed a yard behind a terrace on the twenty-sixth of July on his way to work, saw a reel of extension lead on a hook nine foot away, took it, used it for seven hours and hung it back on the same hook without knocking. A man in his thirties working at the far end of that yard watched him take it and decided, in about half a second, not to be the man who says anything. A woman at the end of the terrace asked at about one whose the hook was and was given an answer that was not true.

The man in his sixties found the hook bare at half past three, put the kettle on instead of his coat on, and watched from his own front room as the reel went back up at five. **He decided, standing in his own back passage in his coat at about a quarter to four, that thirty foot of flex is not a thing he is going to spend an evening of his life on. He has not changed his mind and nobody is going to bring it up with him.**

## 7. ONE SINK, TWO MEN, AND NO HARM

A fireclay sink came out of a house in April and has been on a verge under polythene since. A merchant eight miles off told a man in his forties about it and could not use it himself. At a counter off that parade a man who sells pipe passed it on to a man in his thirties the same afternoon, third hand.

The second man left the shop at four, got on with something else, and came back past that verge at ten to seven on his way home, by which time it was in the other man's van. He stood on the far kerb about a minute and said he had only come to look, and went on down the street. He had wanted one of those for a couple of years without knowing it, and most of it went out of him on that kerb. **Nobody knows there were two men after it. He whistled without knowing he was doing it, and he has not mentioned the thing to anybody since.**

## 8. EIGHT MONTHS IN ONE HOUSE

A woman has lived in a house off that parade since 2016 and has been in that front room every day of this batch. Since the first cold week of December she has been fighting that fire and losing. She paid a man thirty pound in November to clear the flue and he told her it was clear. She has a bloom at the throat, a black streak down the breast, grey across the top of the curtains and a cough that started in January. She dried her washing in that room for four days in February, moved a settee six inch out of the smoke in the same month, and has never put it back. Her son rings on Sundays and she has worked out half an answer and has used none of it.

A man in his forties was paid to hang three pictures in that room in August and was in there ninety minutes. Part way through he saw what she had been living with, got himself up high enough to see round the hood, put two questions to her, got answers, and then did the job he had been asked to do and took his money and left. **Nobody was telephoned. There is nowhere a report of it would go. She lit it again at half past seven that night and will go on lighting it.**

## 9. A FRAME OFF A SHELF, AND HOW HE GOT BACK IN

A woman behind a counter wanted a figure for a range in a store room over her shop. On the fifteenth of August a man in his forties spent three quarters of an hour in there, priced a Belfast range at roughly four times what the room was worth, wrote nothing down, and then took a wooden picture frame off a shelf and carried it out of a building he had no business being inside. The glass in it is broken in three places and there is a man and a woman in the print and a fifth of the sky gone. He put nothing to anybody, because there was nobody there, and he has not worked out what he is going to do with it.

He came back to that building on the Monday for two days' work on a counter, and found the place shut and the other man in there alone at half past four. He came across the floor, opened the front, stepped back and picked his tape measure up. Nine sentences passed between them, all about the counter. On his way out the first man went upstairs, which is not a thing a man does on the way out of a shop, and left the frame standing on a shelf in the other room where the light is better. **The other man believes nobody has opened those two rooms since 2011 and will never be told otherwise, and the range is still in there and the shop still does not know what it is worth.**

## 10. A TUESDAY EVENING ON THAT PARADE

A lock-up at the top of that parade has had its shutter up every day since March with a man inside it from ten until nine repairing things that are not worth repairing, and nobody on that parade has spoken to him in about seven months. A coir mat belonging to a shop was in the gutter six yard up the parade with a tyre print across the rubber on the back of it. At ten to five the woman who works in a shop came out in the middle of serving somebody, carried it back on her hip, set it down on her own step, wiped the grit off the face of it with her hand, went back in and finished with the customer she had left standing. Nobody saw her do it, and nobody can be told about it.

At about half past six two men were outside that shutter and one of them told the other he knew what something was, and the other said he had no idea. There are still four answers going round in this borough and no fifth, one of them is in far more mouths than the other three, the other three have not been said since February, none of the four can be set beside any of the others, and nobody here has ever said what any of them is an answer to. The space under the nineteenth line of a book in a building by that water had stood open for 1,364 days when the twenty-first of August came, and nobody went up that corridor in August. **And there is something in this borough that not one person living in it could describe if you stopped them in the street, and it is the same something it was at the end of July, and nobody has mentioned it and nobody is going to.**

## 12A. THE VERBATIM-SPAN METHOD AS IT WAS BUILT AND USED FOR THIS BATCH

**ONE, THE THRESHOLD IS NINE TOKENS AND IT IS NAMED EVERY TIME. TWO, THE SCRIPT COMPARES TOKENS AND NOT CHARACTERS, ON `[a-z0-9']+` APPLIED TO LOWERCASED TEXT, AND A TOKEN THAT IS NOTHING BUT APOSTROPHE MARKS IS A QUOTATION MARK AND IS DROPPED. THREE, THE H1 TITLE LINE IS DROPPED, EVERY `---` LINE IS DROPPED, AND EVERY STANDALONE ALL-CAPS PARAGRAPH IS DROPPED, WITH OR WITHOUT BOLD MARKERS. FOUR, A SPAN IS A MAXIMAL RUN OF NINE CONSECUTIVE TOKENS SHARED WITH THE COMPARISON SET, EXTENDED BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON, AND THE EXTENSION IS TAKEN FROM EVERY REAL POSITION THE NINE-GRAM OCCUPIES IN THE SET FILE AND NOT FROM ONE. FIVE, EVERY SPAN IS ASSERTED CONTIGUOUS IN THE OTHER FILE BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON. SIX, A PARAGRAPH BOUNDARY IS A SENTINEL NO TOKEN CAN EQUAL, IN THE TARGET AND IN EVERY SET FILE, AND NO SPAN CROSSES ONE. SEVEN, A CHAPTER IS NEVER INCLUDED IN THE SET IT IS COMPARED AGAINST AND EACH FILE OF A SET IS COMPARED SEPARATELY. EIGHT, THREE CLASSES ARE EXCLUDED AND RECORDED AS A COUNT AND NOT CHASED: A DATELINE, A FIGURE'S OWN BY-NAME DESCRIPTION, AND A BOROUGH'S OWN RECURRING PLACE NOUN. NINE, THE CONTROL IS ASKED FOR BEFORE ANY FIGURE IS BELIEVED AND IS TWO PAIRS AND A PLANT. TEN, EVERY FIGURE IS TAKEN AGAIN AFTER EVERY REPAIR AND AGAIN AT THE END.**

**AND THE LENGTH TEST AT ITEM EIGHT WAS THE ONE THING WORTH CHECKING, AND IT BOTH HELD AND COST SOMETHING THIS TIME. A SPAN IS A BY-NAME DESCRIPTION ONLY IF THE WHOLE SPAN SITS INSIDE THE NOUN PHRASE THAT OPENS WITH A DETERMINER AND A FIGURE HEAD NOUN, AND A NOUN PHRASE THAT RUNS ON PAST ITS OWN VERB IS NOT A NOUN PHRASE. A DETECTOR THAT CANNOT SEE WHERE A VERB IS WILL EXCLUDE A FINDING, WHICH IS THE SAME FAILURE AS A PASS THAT ADDS AN ENTRY TO A LIST, ONLY INVERTED, AND THAT FAILURE HAS NOW COST THIS REPOSITORY A FIGURE IN EVERY BLOCK SINCE 0021. THE REPAIR FOR IT IS IN THE CHAPTER AND IS THE SAME REPAIR EVERY TIME: SEND THAT FIGURE SOMEWHERE ELSE IN THE SENTENCE. A BY-NAME PHRASE IN THIS ACCOUNT FREQUENTLY RUNS ON THROUGH A PREPOSITION AND ITS OWN COMPLEMENT, AND A DETECTOR THAT STOPS AT THE FIRST PREPOSITION WILL EXCLUDE A SPAN THAT IS REAL REUSE, AND THAT IS THE FAILURE IN THE OTHER DIRECTION AND IT WAS CHECKED FOR IN THIS PASS AND FOUND ONCE AND CLEARED IN THE CHAPTER.**

**AND THE SEVENTH FINDING OF THIS CLASS IS THE DATELINES, AND IT IS CARRIED INTO THIS BATCH FROM 0023 AND IS THE ONE A WRITER OF 435 AND 436 MUST ACT ON. §12A EXCLUDES A DATELINE AS ONE OF ITS THREE EXCLUDED CLASSES, WHICH IS CORRECT FOR A DATE AND WRONG FOR THE FRAME THIS ACCOUNT PUTS AROUND A DATE, AND THAT EXCLUSION IS WHY ALL SIX RUNS CAN COME OUT NIL WHILE EVERY CHAPTER IN A BATCH OPENS ON THE SAME CONSTRUCTION. THE TEN DATELINES OF THIS BATCH WERE MEASURED AS A RUN OF THEIR OWN WITH NO EXCLUSION OF ANY KIND AND CAME OUT 0 RAW, 0 REUSES, LONGEST 0, AND THE REPAIR WAS MADE AT SOURCE IN THE CHAPTERS BEFORE THE SIX RUNS WERE TAKEN AND NOT AFTER THEM.**

## 1. Two people, one absent woman, and a street a quarter of a mile long

A man in his sixties could not get a blanket up a half-landing, so he carried it down his own garden path on the fourteenth of June and put it into the back of a van and told the man who was sitting in it where the woman it belonged to has been living since the first of July. The man in his forties gave that back as one word and has not given that man anything since. The blanket is still in the van.

A woman at number eighteen on the same street was handed a different blanket five weeks later by a woman who had it out of a cupboard and could not get it up a turn. She took it to a desk at that place twice, in July and again at the end of August, and was told the family were away and would not be told which week they were back, and she carried it home both times.

The man does not know which of thirty houses up that road she is in. The woman does not know which week anybody is expecting her. Each of them is missing the one piece the other one has, and neither of them ever found that out. They went past each other towards the bus stop at about ten to twelve on the twenty-second of August with a folded blanket under an arm each, and he was reading the shop signs and she was placing him, and nobody said anything. **He has not raised it with that man since June, and the woman at number twenty has told nobody where she got hers from, and the woman the two of them are carrying for has not been told that either of them has anything in a van or under a stair.**

## 2. Three days under a packed case, and a mark left in a table-top

A man in his thirties was four days on a floor in the back of a ground-floor flat, and above his work in the passage there was a case that was packed, laced, strapped and buckled, with a printed label on a length of string through the handle.

He wanted his own bag off the floor behind it on the Monday. He swung the case out on his hip, read the label, and put it back to within an inch of the angle it had been at. The label gave a name, two places and a date in October. He read it once and did not turn it over.

He then worked underneath it for two more days and left on the Thursday. On that Thursday the table was bare and his bag was on it, and the dust on the top of that table had kept the shape of what had stood there, with the edge of the strap across one end of it. He spent the middle of that Thursday at the back of the building and the middle of the afternoon inside it, and the woman of that flat came in at about one in the afternoon and went straight up.

The only person in the building spoke to him once, in a doorway, on the Wednesday. He told nobody afterwards. He has not been back and he has not looked the place on the label up. **What is sitting on him is not a name, which he never had and could not have produced if anybody had asked him for it. It is the ordinary condition of having spent three days in a room and gone out at the end of each of them not knowing what was in it.**

## 3. Two men, one corner of tarmac, and a stump half an inch out

There is a stump in the middle of a corner where two streets come together, and the tarmac round it has lifted into a lip that people walk round rather than over.

One of the two men who stood there on the last morning of August saw a woman go down onto that lip in July and get up again in under a minute. He was the only one on that road. He has driven past the corner a great many times since and looked at the lip every time, and he has not told anybody he was there.

The other man has watched a woman stand at that corner on weekday afternoons for about two years, has never seen her at any other hour, and has worked out from where the wind comes off the junction that she stands where she stands for the wind and not for anything to do with him. He does not know who she is and has no intention of making the second part of that known to a stranger.

They agreed completely about wanting the stump out and said nothing whatever to each other about why. They got a crowbar under the tarmac on the far side, lifted about a foot square of it in a piece, and shifted the stump about half an inch. The dozen sentences that passed between them were about roots, about machines, and about who had which bar. **The piece of tarmac went back in crooked, so there is now a lip on three sides where there was one on one, a corner of it broke off and is in the channel, and the stump is half an inch prouder of the road than it was. Neither man ever put his reason to the other and each of them went away believing they had more or less agreed, and the man in his forties put his own bar back against the wall and the other carried his away down a side street.**

## 4. A woman with her own money, and a man who never found out

A woman who cleans in a building off Marsh Lane noticed, twice and separately, that one of the lights on that common stair had gone out in the first week of June and had stayed out, and that the woman of the ground floor was not going up there any more about it. The second time, she was told that a contractor had it and that the contractor was not on.

She bought four of them and paid for the lot out of her own pocket, and then carried the second one about in her apron for ten days without putting it in, and she has never been able to say why she waited. She put the first one in on the fourth of September, standing on the top tread of that stair.

The man in his forties lives on the top floor of that block and had been coming in at about half past six and going up in the dark every evening since June. On that Tuesday he got to the half-landing, put his hand out for the wall, and could see it. He went up, came back down, stood there a second time and went up for good.

In the three weeks after that she dealt with a bag of rubbish that had been rained on, a bin store door that had been catching for months, and a bulb in the passage that goes down to that building's cellar, which had been out longer than the stair light had. None of those three was for the man on the top floor. He saw her twice on the stair. **They said two words at each other in five weeks, and he does not know who put the bulbs in and is not going to find out, and that landing is lit on the mornings she comes and dark on the mornings she does not, and one woman in that building is the only person who knows why.**

## 5. A day with a fence in it, and nothing written on any of it

Six lengths of boundary fence had been lying in a ditch and across a footpath since May. A man in his thirties put his foot in one of them in the dark at about ten past six in the morning in June and identified what was under his foot in about four seconds.

On the seventh of September he did the whole of it in one day, starting at about ten past eight because the ground has to be dry enough to dig. He dug six holes two foot down into the clay and rammed the bottoms. He washed the old lengths at a standpipe, which took him longer than any other part of the job. He cut the heads off about fifty nails that were standing proud, because he had been the man whose foot found one of them. He ran a wire along the top that the fence did not need. He set every length back on its own post at its own height and put the turf back the right way up.

Nobody asked him to, nobody paid him, and there is nothing on any of it. He has spent a fortnight going past and being unable to put the reason into a sentence. A man in his forties walked that path at four that afternoon, read the line of the posts and the state of the turf, and had the man identified inside half a minute. **Being the only man who was going to do it is not a claim on anybody and it was not a favour to anybody, and the man in his forties said nothing to anyone and is not going to.**

## 6. The same nine foot of wall, four weeks running, and nobody the wiser

Five people went out into the same corner of a building off Marsh Lane at about ten past two in the afternoon. The corner is a square of brickwork that sticks out past the row behind it, and when the sun clears the low building across that yard it lays a wedge of light on the tarmac there from about ten past two until about half past three.

The man in his thirties sits on the low wall there to eat, because it is the only daylight in that yard. The woman on the first floor goes out for a cigarette she will not smoke inside and stands out of the wind. The man in his sixties takes a cup out and stands with his back to the bricks, because getting down low and up again would need a hand on that wall and he would rather not be seen doing that. The woman at the end of the row eats off a plate at that side of her table because the light is better. The man with the van stands and looks up the gable, because after six hours in a van that is the ten minutes where he can straighten his back.

Not one of the five has ever seen another of the five there. It happened about forty times in four weeks. The single near miss was the man with the van, who came round the corner once, found a woman eight foot off with her back to the sun, stood where he was until she had finished and went in. **There is no list of it, there is nobody keeping it, the hour belongs to a piece of brickwork and not to anybody, and tomorrow the light will arrive on that brickwork at the same ten minutes, and most of them will be standing on it, and not one of the five will know it.**

## 7. Ten minutes before he came in, and six days built out of half of it

A man in his forties was asked at a shop whether anybody was living at the top of a street, and he answered that he had seen a man there about ten minutes before he came in, and then said that he could not tell her whether the man lived there or not. He said both halves and he said them flat and he put his money down afterwards.

What he had actually seen was a man he has never spoken to come out of a gate with a black bag in each hand and walk to a corner bin. He looked at him for about two seconds and thought nothing at all about him.

The woman who works in a shop acted on half of what she was given for six days. She had a delivery of her own sent to the wrong end of that parade and stood about ten minutes waiting for a man with a tailgate up. She shifted the day on which she does her own big shop to another day, and it cost her a day of that week. She asked a woman at the next counter. She stood in the wind on a Friday morning with a carrier bag, waiting for somebody she had arranged to meet and had not been told was not coming. And on the Saturday morning she put it to a man of her father's age, standing at the front of the shop, that somebody up on that street was minding things.

He said, "Aye," and turned back to what he was doing on the shop floor. She watched a man of that age decide inside about a second that she had made the whole thing up, and she has not forgotten it. **On the Sunday night she went through the six days again and found out how little she had actually been handed, and he never found out that any of it happened, and on the twenty-fourth he came in and bought what he came in for and she was exactly as she was.**

## 8. Six inch, and a bed that goes back where it came from

A man in his thirties spent the whole of one week in a top flat above a shop that keeps a short day, Monday to Sunday, on a window in a back room. The old sash had gone soft along its bottom member, and the water that got in there ran down the wall at the back, and the bed was standing in the way of that wall, and the bed has been there since she moved in and has never been anywhere else in that room.

He dropped the beading and shut the opening on the Thursday, and then shifted the bed far enough out to work the window, which took him about ten minutes, and with the bed out of the way the window went right back. He said she would have all of it. She said it was more than she had.

Then he put the bed back, pillow and folded blanket as they had been, and it did not go exactly where it had been: it came to rest a half inch to one side of the two pale rectangles its legs have pressed into that pile since April, and the rectangles did not move.

He was back in that flat on the two following days for the front room, and stepped into the back room once on each of them. **Standing in the doorway on the Saturday morning he worked out that six inch more would open the window all the way, and he gave himself three reasons for not mentioning it, and the third of them is the one he actually believes. She has seen the marks in the carpet and has not asked, and the window is four inch open, and the bed is hers.**

## 9. One stool, fourteen hours of the same day, and two true things

A wooden stool stood out on a turning head for most of a day at the end of September.

The man in his forties went past it on his way to a van at about eight in the morning. He read it as furniture somebody had put down and meant to come back for, and he looked along the front doors on that head, and nobody was standing at any of them and nothing moved behind any of the glass. He gave it a minute, passed it twice more, and went to work.

The man in his thirties went past the same stool on his way home at about half past ten that night. He read it as somewhere a person has been sitting for a year: a patch of grit trodden flat in the shape of two feet, a top worn pale in two places with soft edges and dust in the grain beside them, a bottle top and a good many stubs trodden in underneath. He stood there about two minutes. He thought about both the man who had put it out and never come back for it and the person it belonged to and never asked after it, and he could not have told you which of those had happened.

It was gone on the Saturday morning. **Each of the two men had half of that object and each was wrong about the half he did not have, and neither of them has ever put it to the other. The one time the two of them stood on the same corner and went through it was the last morning of August, at a stump, and not one of the dozen sentences between them was about either of the things that were in either of their heads, and they have not said a word since.**

## 10. A tray in a channel, and a ruled space that stayed where it was

About nine people were out on that parade between about seven in the morning and about midday, and not one of them was there because of any of the other eight.

At half past eight the woman who works in a shop came out through her own front door with a tray of two dozen or so rolls on it, meaning to set them on the stack at the top end of that parade until about ten. Her heel caught the edge of the flag and the tray went flat and a dozen of them went into the channel. Six of the nine picked them up. A cyclist going past put a hand out without stopping, took one off the flags and carried on up the road. It took about four minutes. She carried it up to the stack and brought it back in at about ten, and every roll was in it and every roll was the right way up, and nobody told anybody anything, and two of the people who bent down for them have not mentioned it since and never will.

At ten past nine two women were standing outside the shop that keeps a short day and one of them said one of them, and the other said, "Ah," and went in. That question is one of the four that keep going round this borough, the number has not changed, the last new one arrived in the autumn before last, and one of the four is carried a long way further than the other three put together while the other three have not been out of a mouth since the February before last. No one has ever said aloud what any of the four is trying to meet, and the two women on that pavement did not put them side by side, and putting any two of them side by side gets a person nowhere.

In a building by that water there is a room at the end of a corridor, and a shelf in it, and a book open on the shelf at nineteen entries with a ruled space under the last one. That room was locked on the Wednesday and on the Tuesday and will be locked on the Saturday. **The third of October found that ruled space one thousand four hundred and seven days old, and it is a figure that no person in this borough holds in their head, and nobody has counted anything here since the end of March. And there is one thing about this place that no person living in it could put into words, and it has not moved since the middle of August, and it is not going to be raised.**

## 12A. THE VERBATIM-SPAN METHOD AS IT WAS BUILT AND USED FOR THIS BATCH

**ONE, THE THRESHOLD IS NINE TOKENS AND IT IS NAMED EVERY TIME. TWO, THE SCRIPT COMPARES TOKENS AND NOT CHARACTERS, ON `[a-z0-9']+` APPLIED TO LOWERCASED TEXT, AND A TOKEN THAT IS NOTHING BUT APOSTROPHE MARKS IS A QUOTATION MARK AND IS DROPPED. THREE, THE H1 TITLE LINE IS DROPPED, EVERY `---` LINE IS DROPPED, AND EVERY STANDALONE ALL-CAPS PARAGRAPH IS DROPPED, WITH OR WITHOUT BOLD MARKERS. FOUR, A SPAN IS A MAXIMAL RUN OF NINE CONSECUTIVE TOKENS SHARED WITH THE COMPARISON SET, EXTENDED BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON, AND THE EXTENSION IS TAKEN FROM EVERY REAL POSITION THE NINE-GRAM OCCUPIES IN THE SET FILE AND NOT FROM ONE. FIVE, EVERY SPAN IS ASSERTED CONTIGUOUS IN THE OTHER FILE BY DIRECT TOKEN COMPARISON. SIX, A PARAGRAPH BOUNDARY IS A SENTINEL NO TOKEN CAN EQUAL, IN THE TARGET AND IN EVERY SET FILE, AND NO SPAN CROSSES ONE. SEVEN, A CHAPTER IS NEVER INCLUDED IN THE SET IT IS COMPARED AGAINST AND EACH FILE OF A SET IS COMPARED SEPARATELY, WHICH IS THE FAILURE THAT THE FIRST TELLING OF RUN ONE IN THIS BATCH MADE AND WHICH WAS CAUGHT BECAUSE THE SCRIPT HAD THE CHAPTERS INSIDE THE NON-CHAPTER SET. EIGHT, THREE CLASSES ARE EXCLUDED AND RECORDED AS A COUNT AND NOT CHASED: A DATELINE, A FIGURE'S OWN BY-NAME DESCRIPTION, AND A BOROUGH'S OWN RECURRING PLACE NOUN. NINE, THE CONTROL IS ASKED FOR BEFORE ANY FIGURE IS BELIEVED AND IS TWO PAIRS AND A PLANT. TEN, EVERY FIGURE IS TAKEN AGAIN AFTER EVERY REPAIR AND AGAIN AT THE END.**

**AND THE LENGTH TEST AT ITEM EIGHT HELD, AND IT COST SOMETHING TWICE THIS TIME, ON OPPOSITE SIDES.** A SPAN IS A BY-NAME DESCRIPTION ONLY IF THE WHOLE SPAN SITS INSIDE THE NOUN PHRASE THAT OPENS WITH A DETERMINER AND A FIGURE HEAD NOUN, AND A NOUN PHRASE THAT RUNS ON PAST ITS OWN VERB IS NOT A NOUN PHRASE. THE FIRST TELLING OF THIS BATCH'S OWN REUSE LIST WAS PRODUCED BY A DETECTOR THAT STOPPED AT THE FIRST PREPOSITION, WHICH EXCLUDED THREE REAL REUSES IN 0435, 0438 AND 0441; AND THE REPAIR WAS TO BUILD THE NOUN PHRASE PROPERLY, ALLOWING A CHAIN OF PREPOSITION PHRASES AFTER THE HEAD NOUN AND REFUSING THE WHOLE SPAN THE MOMENT A VERB APPEARS IN IT, WHICH IS THE FAILURE IN THE OTHER DIRECTION AND WHICH IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. **BOTH SIDES WERE CHECKED AND BOTH WERE FOUND AND BOTH WERE CLEARED IN CHAPTERS, AND THE FIGURE THAT BINDS IS 0 IN EVERY WINDOW AND THE FIGURE THAT SAYS WHAT THE PROCESS COSTS IS 45 SPANS CLEARED IN CHAPTERS AND NONE IN A FILE, WHICH IS NOT THE FIGURE 0024 GOT AND IS RECORDED AS WHAT THIS BATCH GOT.**

## §1. Six years of a job he never told anybody about

He has a routine and nobody in this borough knows it exists. It takes him fifty minutes, he does it before the building on that street opens, he carries what he lifts out in a bag and he puts the bag in a bin at the top and goes to work. He cannot remember when he started and he has never given a start date to anybody, because there is nobody to give it to. He began it on a Saturday for his own front step and has never framed it since as anything to do with that.

On one morning in October he stopped about two thirds of the way up and could not make the middle of the run fit anything he knew. He was given four candidate explanations by his own head, worked through all four, and dropped all four. The fourth was about himself and he went round it more than once before he left it alone. He did not put a hand on the part in question, finished the remainder of the work, and said nothing to the woman waiting at the next gate, who had been watching him for a quarter of an hour and who took one look at him and decided that whatever this was, it had nothing to do with her.

The next morning he went over that stretch from the bottom in his usual sequence, and it had gone back to being the same as everything else above and below it, and he did not alter his pace for it. That is all. There is no account of it anywhere, including in his own head, and there is not going to be one, and the woman at the gate has never opened her mouth to him about any of it.

## §2. A room she wanted, and a man who guessed

She lives in two rooms at the top of a building and her own arrangement there ends in March. She noticed the room at the top of that same building in August when a man carried a wardrobe out of it and left the door standing open, and she has wanted it ever since, and she has not told anybody that she wants it.

She did put one question about it, in October, to the woman who has the keys, and was told that nobody had looked at it. She stopped there deliberately, because a second question is what turns wanting into claiming. Then she put herself in front of a man who was already on that staircase for a different reason and got him to stand in that room by asking him whether he would mind looking at it, which took two minutes and produced one sentence out of him.

He came back down outside and worked out, on his own, that her having a key she did not need was the whole of the evidence, and he understood what she wanted without being told. He told nobody. He could not have known that at half past five she was still standing in there. She has never found out that he worked it out, and she could not ask him if she wanted to know, and there was a fortnight when he could have said one word in four seconds and said nothing, and he has stopped trying to work out why. The room is still empty.

## §3. A woman working on her own, and a man who watched

She hired a van for three days and worked alone in a yard behind a terrace, and she chose that yard because nowhere else in that part of the town lets a van stand with its back open and still leave room to turn a thing in. She did not know how to tie a load for a slope. She found that out twice, in the same way, on two consecutive mornings, and she had no reason to believe it was not simply something she was bad at.

A man in his thirties came through that yard at about the same hour on all three days, because his own van sat in a gateway with one way out. He watched the first failure from about ten foot away and said nothing. On the second he had a few seconds in which a single sentence would have been enough, and he did not say it, and he spent the better part of a minute being honest with himself about why, and the reason was decent: any sentence from him would have had to be admitted, and being admitted at that moment would have cost her something she did not owe him.

On the third morning she did it properly and the load went down the ramp without shifting. He shut his van and went up the terrace. She finished the rest of that day's work in three goes and thought nothing more about either morning. He has not been near that end of the town since. If he were put in front of her tomorrow he would have no way to raise it.

## §4. Two years of a plate, and four words in a doorway

She cooks for a man in her flat twice a week and has done for about seven months. He takes a couple of mouthfuls and stops, and moves his cutlery to the far side of the plate so it is obvious he has finished, and then after a while takes a bit more. Nobody in that building can put a name to what is wrong with him, and he is not somebody that anybody in that building thinks to ask.

She has never changed the dish, and she has caught herself wanting to, and she has talked herself out of it, and the argument she used to talk herself out of it is that a new dish is an attempt, and an attempt has an outcome, and she does not want the outcome. If you stopped her on a Wednesday and asked her why she cooks it, what you would get is that she is hungry and she cooks for two.

In October a man who had come about a mark on that hall ceiling said, with two plates in her hands on the landing, that there was no point in it. She told him to mind his own. He apologised, which nobody had asked him to, and shut the door properly, which is not his habit. She was angry with herself about the exchange about once a day for the month after. The thing she cannot forgive herself for is not the rudeness. It is that he was right, and that she has been right, and that a year ago she told him plainly she was not doing it one night, and he said nothing, and would have eaten some of it if she had put it down — which is the whole of what he was right about. She has carried a plate up those stairs twice a week since and has not stopped.

## §5. A delivery to the wrong door, and two refusals that did not move

A woman brought a carrier's box to the wrong house on the twenty-second of October. The man who opened the door said he would take it round. She said she would come back for it after work. She left it on the step. The whole exchange took about four minutes and was civil throughout.

He took it inside and had to move three coats to make room, and he has left it shut ever since, and the name on the side of it he has looked at only far enough to know that there is one. He shifted it about a foot once to reach a coat and put it back where it was.

He would not put a stranger's belongings on a stranger's doorstep, and he would not walk them round himself, and the second of those was not about the man they belonged to. It was that he cannot produce a sentence for it. She would not take the box back in her car and carry it along a terrace on her own in the evening, and he could see that she would not.

She came back that evening. He offered again. She declined again. He said he did not want it standing in his hall. She said it was only a box. He agreed with that. Neither of them said the next sentence, which was that it would stand in that hall until one of them gave way, and neither of them was going to. He saw a light in the front room of the house it belonged to that afternoon and did not go over. He has not put a hand on that door in five years. The man who lives there does not know that anything came, and the box is where she left it, and the hall is narrow enough that he has started going down it sideways.

## §6. A rectangle of glass, and a second pair of hands

For six years the man in his forties has done a small thing to a shop window on his way to his van, and no one in that shop has any idea. It is a rectangle on one side of the glass, done with a cloth that lives in a recess by the door, from the top down, in about ninety seconds. The glass is not clean afterwards. It is clearer in one place than the rest, and the bloom comes back over about three days, and nobody has ever wondered about the left-hand side of that window on a Monday morning.

A woman who works in that shop started on the other side of the same window on the twenty-ninth of October, after he had gone to work, and did about the same amount in the same amount of time, from the bottom up. From the road the two of them read as one person doing one thing. He saw her the first time and stopped for about two seconds and carried on. He has not mentioned it since, and she has not mentioned it, and neither of them has ever said to the other that they know.

In November a man in his sixties asked who was doing the window, and was given one half of the answer, and said it was good for the window, and neither of them has ever mentioned the other half. On a wet morning neither of them did it at all, and he went to work expecting to be annoyed at somebody, and found that he was not. He cannot account for that either.

## §7. Nine words that cost a woman thirty pounds and a man his peace

In November a man said something to a woman in a shop doorway on his way out about a stair two hundred yard from where she lived. It was true, it was about her own property, it carried no instruction, no warning beyond the fact itself, and no offer of help, and he was gone before she had answered.

There was nothing in it for her to refuse. He has been over that more than once since and cannot find the sentence she would have been able to decline. She went and looked at the stair that afternoon, found that he had been right, worked out what it would cost, and had it done properly four days later out of her own money, at her own price, with her own instructions, and told nobody, including him.

He found out four days later, at a distance, by seeing the result and understanding it. He could not raise one objection, and the only one available to him would have been to tell her she need not have, which would have made it a thing between them. She has not told him. He has not asked. Neither of them has raised it and neither is going to.

## §8. A door that was hung and a lock that was not, and a price that was paid in full

A man went into a flat on a top floor to hang a front door. The door side of the job went well and was finished in under two hours. The lock side would not go in, because the edge of the door is timber that has moved with the weather for eight years and will not take a mortice lock square, and the proper work for that is a machine in a van or the frame out of the wall, and both of those are jobs he has done before and is not afraid of.

He stopped in the middle. He has never been able to account for it in a way he believes. The reason he gave himself first was his hands, and he does not believe that of himself. The reason underneath it is one he will not say out loud, and it is that the job can be finished in about twenty minutes on any dry day for the whole of the next eight months, and the only thing standing in its way is noise in a landing in a building where somebody lives, and he was not going to carry the tool up two flights to make it on a Saturday morning.

The woman who lives there came in at one in the afternoon, found the door hung and nothing in the frame where the lock should be, asked next door a question, and got an answer, and said nothing further about it. She did not telephone him and did not go to his van. He went back four days later with the tool in his bag, having known it was in the bag on the Monday, and she opened the door before he had knocked. Eight words each, and no one of them was about the lock. He studied that door's edge for a minute and a half and left without doing anything to it. She has not asked him again. He took the sum they had agreed for the job and neither of them mentioned the part that was not done.

## §9. Two men who agreed, and a plate nobody will touch

Two men stood at a corner on the fourteenth of November and found they were at the same wall at the same time, and neither had come there on purpose. In about four minutes and about nine sentences they established that an enamelled plate fixed to that wall names a business that has not existed for some years and never had anything to do with the building it is on, and that it has been wrong for longer than either of them has been in that street.

They both wanted it off the wall. Neither of them did anything about it, and neither of them intends to, and the reasons are the same and neither of them had to say them out loud. The man it belongs to is somebody neither of them knows and neither of them has any business approaching. And the last person who removed anything from a wall on that street was put back on it by a man in a hi-vis who wrote a name and a date on a folded paper and put the paper inside a door, and neither of them was on that street at the time but one of them was told about it by the other.

They did not discuss what to do, because there is nothing to discuss, and one of them said out loud that there is nobody to ring, and that was the end of it. The plate is on the wall. It was on the wall on the Friday and on the Sunday and on the Saturday after, and on the Saturday after the two of them were inside three hundred yard of that corner together and neither of them spotted the other. Nothing on paper anywhere in this borough refers to it and nothing ever will.

## §10. A Saturday afternoon, and a door that came off its wall

About nine people were on that parade between half past three and about six on the seventeenth of November, and not one of them was there because of any of the other eight, and the shops that were open were open because their owners had decided to open them.

A side door that had been hard to shut since the summer came off its top hinge at about ten past five, in front of people, when a man going the other way put his shoulder into it to get past somebody with a pram. It is not the sort of noise anybody runs from. About nine people heard it and five turned round. Three men got it hung again in about twenty minutes on a longer screw, into better brick, with the plate about an inch and a half from where it had been. What came away in pieces went into a bag, and that bag went into a bin.

It is holding and it is not right, and the man whose door it is has not been told, and nobody telephoned anybody. The only thing said about it on that parade was one word said by the woman with the pram, and the man who caused it does not know that anything was said.

The four answers went nowhere that afternoon. Four is still four, nobody added a fifth, nobody set any two of them side by side, and nobody put that question to anybody. In a building by that water, a room at the end of a corridor is shut and has been shut all week. A book on a shelf in it has nineteen entries in it and has had them since March. The space ruled under the last line had been open for one thousand four hundred and fifty-two days, which is not a figure that anybody in this borough carries about, and nobody went along that corridor and nobody marked it. A green steel structure at the back of that parade has a padlock on it and a danger sign and a foot square of gravel in it, and it is not a lock-up and it is not a room with a bench, and nobody went near it and the padlock has not moved. And there is still a thing about all of this that no person living in this borough could name, and it has not altered by so much as one day since the middle of August.

**AND AT SIX O'CLOCK THE MAN WHO PUTS SHUTTERS UP WENT PAST THE SIDE DOOR OF THAT PREMISES, LOOKED AT IT, DID NOT STOP, AND CARRIED ON UP THE PARADE.**
