## §12E. THE EIGHT FINDINGS OF THE REVIEW OF 0032, AND WHAT THIS BLOCK DID WITH EACH OF THEM

1. **A CHAPTER CAN USE AN OBJECT ITS OWN CARD FORBIDS.** The checker was copied, its lists were changed, and it was run on each chapter as it was written rather than at the end. **FIVE CHAPTERS OUT OF FIVE WERE CAUGHT ON THE FIRST PASS, AT 22 HITS, AND ALL 22 WERE CLEARED IN THE CHAPTERS.** The finding is turned into a tool and the tool is load-bearing, and the figure is a third of 0033's, for the reason at §12C item 2.
2. **A WRITER CAN PUT ITS OWN ARGUMENT WITH ITS OWN CARD ON THE PAGE.** A sentence that explains why a thing is not a violation is itself a sentence that is not in the book. **ONE SELF-CORRECTING DASH WAS WRITTEN IN 0528 IN DRAFTING AND IS ON THE PAGE NOW NOWHERE, AND NO CARD WAS DEFENDED TO KEEP ONE.**
3. **A CARD CAN PRINT A FIGURE THAT IS ON THE CLOSED LIST, A DATE ITS OWN CALENDAR DOES NOT REACH, OR A WORD IN THE SETTING IT ASKS FOR.** Five of this block's ten cards do one of those things, and they are at §12D items 1 to 5. **THE RULE IS UNCHANGED AND IT IS THE 0030 RULE: A CHAPTER BEATS A CARD, A CHAPTER ON THE PAGE BEATS A LATER CHAPTER, AND A CARD NEVER BEATS EITHER.**
4. **A DURATION THAT DISAGREES WITH ITS OWN DATELINE.** Seven were wrong and all seven were corrected in the chapters, and the list is at §12C item 8. **NO CHAPTER OF THIS BLOCK SPANS TWO DATES.**
5. **A SINGLE ORDINARY WORD CAN BECOME ONE CHAPTER'S FILLER, AND A MEASURE THAT NAMES THE WRONG WORD IS NOT A FINDING EITHER.** See §13. **THE DECLARED MEASURE FOR THIS BLOCK IS *QUITE*, WHICH IS NEITHER *ONE* NOR *WEEK* NOR *ABOUT*, AND IT CAME OUT AT 5 ACROSS THE FIVE. THE MEASURE 0032 DECLARED, *ONE*, IS REPORTED BESIDE IT AT 49. THE MEASURE 0033 DECLARED, *WEEK*, IS REPORTED BESIDE THAT AT 6. AND THE WORD THE 0032 REVIEW FOUND DOING THE WORK, *ABOUT*, IS REPORTED BESIDE ALL THREE AT 131, OF WHICH 95 ARE *ABOUT* PLUS A QUANTITY.** ALL FOUR ARE REPORTED AND EVERY CHAPTER IS COUNTED AND EVERY PLACE IS GIVEN AT §13.
6. **THE SECOND TELLING OF RUN FOUR IS BIGGER THAN THE FIRST.** It was anticipated rather than discovered: §1 to §10 of this block, §1 to §10 of the open-threads block and the character-state roster were all written as ledgers of dispositions grouped by person, before any measurement was taken against a state file. **THE FIGURE THAT BINDS IS THE LAST ONE AT §13A ITEM 4 AND IT IS NIL.**
7. **NINE CARDS OUT OF TEN CAN NAME A PLACE IN THE RESISTANCE COLUMN.** The resistance columns of this block's ten cards were read before a chapter was written. **FOUR NAME A PLACE, 0525, 0526, 0527 AND 0528, AGAINST A BUDGET OF THREE, AND THE OVERRUN IS IN THE CARDS AND NOT IN THE CHAPTERS, AND WHAT ELSE COULD HAVE BEEN THE RESISTANCE IS RECORDED CARD BY CARD AT §11 OF THE 0034 OPEN-THREADS BLOCK.** THE FIGURE IS FOUR, WHICH IS WORSE THAN 0032's TWO, 0033's TWO AND 0030's NINE, AND IT WAS NOT ARRANGED.
8. **A COUNT OF GAPS IN A TEN-CHAPTER RUN IS NOT A CONSTANT.** The count was made from the chapter dates and not from any prompt, on the second telling, and it is ten, and the prompt's own rule is carried forward as binding only for a run that contains a two-day chapter.

## §12G. THE REVIEW OF CONTINUATION 0034, ITS NINE FINDINGS, AND WHAT WAS DONE WITH EACH OF THEM

**A REVIEW RAN ON CHAPTERS 525 TO 529 AND THEIR SIX STATE FILES AFTER THIS BLOCK WAS FIRST DRAFTED. IT FOUND NINE THINGS. FOUR WERE IN THE CHAPTERS, FOUR WERE IN THE STATE FILES, AND ONE WAS A MIS-DESCRIPTION OF A CHAPTER IN A STATE FILE, AND ALL NINE WERE REPAIRED AT THE SOURCE. NO DATE, NO DAY-COUNT, NO CARD, NO FLAG, NO MAJOR TURN AND NO CHAPTER'S PLOT WAS TOUCHED, AND NO CHAPTER WAS RESTARTED, AND THE FIVE THAT EXIST ARE THE FIVE THAT WERE THERE.**

1. **A NAMED WEEKDAY CONTRADICTING ITS OWN DATELINE, IN A CLOSING ALL-CAPS BLOCK.** 0526 is Tuesday the twenty-ninth of October 2019 in its own dateline and in its own body, and its closing block said *IT IS THE FIRST WEDNESDAY SINCE MARCH*. **THE WEEKDAY IS NOW TUESDAY, AND THE CLAIM WAS ALSO NARROWED FROM SOMEBODY TO THE TWO OF THEM, BECAUSE A TUESDAY ON WHICH SOMEBODY IN THIS BOROUGH SAYS NOTHING TO ANYBODY IS NOT A THING THAT CAN BE TRUE.** No other sentence in the chapter changed and the whole weight of the ending is the same.
2. **TWO HOUSE-NUMBER SYSTEMS IN ONE CHAPTER.** 0528's opening all-caps block said the house was number twenty-six and its own body said number sixteen in six places, and the neighbour was number eighteen twice and then number twenty-eight twice. **THE CAPS BLOCK NOW SAYS SIXTEEN AND THE NEIGHBOUR IS EIGHTEEN THROUGHOUT, AND THE ROW RUNS TWELVE, FOURTEEN, SIXTEEN, EIGHTEEN, WHICH IS THE ONLY ORDERING THE CHAPTER HAD ALREADY.** The house has been empty since 2011 in both tellings, so nothing about the plot moved.
3. **A DISCLOSURE'S OWN WEEKDAY CONTRADICTING ITSELF.** 0528 dated the telling to the Tuesday of the fifth of November, which is a Tuesday, and then referred to it twenty lines later as a Wednesday. **IT IS NOW A TUESDAY IN BOTH PLACES, AND THE REASON THE TELLING CARRIES ANYTHING AT ALL IS STILL IN THE CHAPTER, WHICH IS THAT THE WOMAN WHO TOLD IT IS EIGHTY-ONE AND IS COUNTING HER OWN REMAINING TUESDAYS.**
4. **A REVEAL WHOSE PAYLOAD POSTDATES ITS OWN UTTERANCE.** 0528 dated a sentence overheard in the middle of October 1999 and then used it to prove a decision made in November 1999, which no sentence can do, and its ninth line called the whole matter the October of 1999 while the argument it turns on was fought in September of 1999. **THE NINTH LINE NOW SAYS SEPTEMBER OF 1999, WHICH IS WHERE THE SURGERY VISIT AND THE ARGUMENT NIGHT ARE, AND THE FORTY-FIFTH LINE NO LONGER NAMES A MONTH AT ALL AND INSTEAD SAYS THE DECISION WAS MADE IN THE WEEKS BETWEEN THAT NIGHT AND THE MIDDLE OF OCTOBER, WHICH IS THE ONLY SPAN THE SENTENCE CAN COVER.** The reveal is unchanged: the sister who argued for the staying had already arranged to do the moving herself, and said so out loud to nobody, and then said the opposite in front of everybody for twelve years.
5. **THREE INCOMPATIBLE FLOORS FOR 0530, TWO OF WHICH CALL A SUNDAY A WEDNESDAY.** `state/current.md` told the writer of 0530 that it may not be dated before Wednesday the twentieth of October 2019, and the twentieth of October 2019 was a Sunday; `state/batch-summaries.md` gave the twentieth of October as a floor in the same sentence as a three-to-seven-day gap from the thirteenth of November, which the floor itself violates; and this block named the thirtieth of October in two places, which is after the date it is a floor for. **ALL THREE NOW CARRY THE SAME FIGURE, WHICH IS THE ONE THE GAP GIVES: 0530 IS DATED FROM SATURDAY THE SIXTEENTH OF NOVEMBER 2019 TO WEDNESDAY THE TWENTIETH OF NOVEMBER 2019 INCLUSIVE, THREE TO SEVEN DAYS FROM 0529's OWN WEDNESDAY THE THIRTEENTH OF NOVEMBER, AND THE BATCH'S OWN FLOOR OF THURSDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH OF OCTOBER 2019 STANDS SEPARATELY FOR ALL TEN CHAPTERS. THIS WAS THE HIGHEST-VALUE FINDING IN THE REVIEW BECAUSE THE 0530 WRITER READS `state/current.md` FIRST.**
6. **A MISSPELLING IN THIS BLOCK THAT NOBODY SAW AND THAT A GREP COULD NOT HAVE FOUND.** The thirtieth of October is spelled *TWIRTIETH* in both of the sentences at §0 and §16 that the review quoted, and the review quoted them as correct. **BOTH SENTENCES WERE REWRITTEN, SO THE MISSPELLING IS GONE WITH THEM, AND IT IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE A FIGURE THAT LOOKS RIGHT ON THE SCREEN CAN BE WRONG IN THE FILE, AND EVERY REPLACEMENT IN THIS REPAIR WAS MADE BY MATCHING INSIDE THE FILE AND NOT BY EYES.**

## §1. The condition of the people of this block, grouped by person and not by chapter

**EVERY ENTRY BELOW IS A DISPOSITION AND NOT A FINDING, AND THE ORDER OF THE FIVE CHAPTERS IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. A LEDGER THAT WALKS FIVE CHAPTERS IN ORDER IS A TRANSCRIPTION, AND THE FIGURE THAT COSTS IS AT §13A ITEM 4 BELOW AND AT ITEM 4 OF THE BLOCK ABOVE.**

- **THE MAN IN HIS MID FORTIES AND THE WOMAN IN HER EARLY FORTIES WHO HAVE LIVED AT THE SAME ADDRESS SINCE 2008.** He gave a woman he works with a wrong year in a corridor in October and cannot put it behind him. In the first half of November he put it to her, she took a week over it, and on the fifteenth she went out for forty minutes and did not say where. On the twentieth he went into the small bathroom for the first time in years, put his thumb on a word in the middle of the field, took it off, and put the chalk down squared to the edge. **HE MAY NOT BE ASKED WHY HE WENT IN, HE MAY NOT BE ASKED WHY HE DID NOT READ IT, AND THE MARK HIS OWN HAND MADE IS SPENT AS AN OBJECT AND AS A THING.**
- **THE WOMAN IN HER EARLY FORTIES.** She has put one word down every night since the March of 2008, in white chalk, on a mirror nobody has cleaned in the same period, and she reads the year back in the last week of November. She put it where he would find it and has told nobody, including him. **SHE MAY NOT BE ASKED WHY SHE LEFT IT, THE MIRROR, THE CHALK, THE READING AND THE ANNUAL NIGHT ARE SPENT AS OBJECTS AND AS A THING, AND HER REASON IS NOT TO BE PUT INTO HER MOUTH FOR HER.**
- **THE MAN OF ABOUT SIXTY-ONE AND THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-ONE WHO HAVE PLAYED CROQUET ON A SHUT GREEN EVERY SUNDAY SINCE THE MARCH OF 2013.** On the twenty-fourth of November the younger one brought a man he has known since the middle of 2017, said nothing about it, and the older one had it worked out inside a few seconds and walked off the green a little over an hour afterwards and said nothing about that either. **NEITHER MAY BE ASKED WHY THE THIRD MAN WAS BROUGHT, NEITHER MAY BE ASKED WHY THE MALLET WENT DOWN, AND THE GREEN, THE HUT, THE MALLLETS, THE THIRD HOOP, THE NINE SENTENCES AND THE HOUR AND A QUARTER ARE SPENT AS OBJECTS AND AS A THING.**
- **THE MAN OF ABOUT FORTY-ONE WHO WAS BROUGHT TO THAT GREEN.** He does not know that he was brought to be looked at, he does not know what either of the other two is carrying, he apologised twice and won a game and asked one question about how long it had been going on. **HE IS NOT A WITNESS TO ANYTHING, HE MAY NOT BE ASKED AGAIN, AND HE MAY NOT BE TOLD.**
- **THE CARETAKER OF THE HUT.** He has not asked about the mallets once. **HE IS NOT A WITNESS AND IS NOT TO BE ASKED ABOUT THE GREEN.**
- **THE WOMAN OF ABOUT SIXTY-TWO AND THE MAN OF ABOUT SIXTY-FIVE WHO HAVE BEEN IN THAT HOUSE SINCE 1989.** She has put a pair of spectacles back where she finds them since 2016; he has been putting them back folded on a sill before she is up since the Friday before the twenty-eighth of November; she went down on purpose before he was up and he had already been down and gone back up. She has worked out what the early mornings are really for, and he knows she has worked it out. **NEITHER MAY BE ASKED WHY HE GETS UP, THE SENTENCE, THE THREE PLACES, THE SILL, THE FOLD AND THE EIGHT DAYS ARE SPENT AS OBJECTS AND AS A THING.**
- **THE MAN OF ABOUT SIXTY-FIVE.** He is a younger man for three quarters of an hour every morning, and in eight days he has not once turned the question of what she makes of it. **HE MAY NOT BE ASKED WHY HE PUTS THEM BACK, HE MAY NOT BE TOLD THAT SHE KNOWS WHY, AND WHAT HE WAS NOT ASKED IS NOT TO BE PUT INTO HIS MOUTH FOR HIM.**
- **THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-TWO AND THE WOMAN OF ABOUT FIFTY.** Twenty-five years ago she asked him for three hours of an evening in a house in the town. He gave her an hour. He was not there for it and sent nothing. She has assumed for twenty-five years that he did not want to, and he has known that since the week after. A third man said in front of both of them in August that he would have said it was the first man all along, and said the same thing again in December, four months later, in the same voice. **NEITHER MAY BE ASKED ABOUT 1994, THE PROMISE IS SPENT AND IS NOT TO BE REPEATED, AND IT IS NOT TO BE ARRANGED THAT EITHER OF THEM SAYS IT OUT LOAD.**
- **THE MAN IN HIS LATE FORTIES WHO HAS KNOWN THE FIRST OF THEM SINCE 2008.** He said the sentence twice, four months apart, and neither time knew what he was doing. **HE IS NOT A WITNESS, HE IS NOT TO BE TOLD, AND HE MAY NOT BE USED A THIRD TIME TO CARRY A DISCLOSURE.**
- **THE MAN IN HIS EARLY SEVENTIES WHO PUTS GRIT IN THE DIP AT THE BOTTOM OF A RAMP IN A BLOCK OF NINE FLATS.** He has done it every morning for nine years, he went to his daughter's in the middle of November and will not be in this borough again until well into January, and nobody in that building has ever mentioned it. **HE IS NOT TO BE WRITTEN BACK INTO, THE RAMP, THE DIP, THE GRIT, THE NINE FLATS, THE SHUTTER AND THE THREE WEEKS AWAY ARE SPENT AS OBJECTS AND AS A THING.**
- **THE WOMAN OF ABOUT EIGHTY-ONE WHO USES A FRAME AND GOES ROUND THE WHOLE OF THE BLOCK TO REACH THE OTHER END.** She has had to do it a dozen times or more this side of Christmas, and on the seventh of December she found the dip gritted and went back up the ramp and said nothing. **SHE MAY NOT BE ASKED WHY SHE GOES ROUND, THE FRAME, THE RAMP AND THE DOZEN TIMES ARE SPENT AS OBJECTS AND AS A THING.**
- **THE MAN IN THE THIRD FLAT WHO CAME OUT FOR FOUR MINUTES WITH A SHOVEL OF HIS OWN.** He did the whole width twice over, banked the grit to the sides of the dip and not into the middle of it, turned round and went back in, and does not know he did it the way the other man does it. **HE IS NOT A WITNESS, HE IS NOT TO BE ASKED, AND HE MAY NOT BE TOLD THAT HE DID IT THE OTHER MAN'S WAY.**

## §12E. THE FINDINGS OF THE REVIEW OF 525–529, WHICH THIS BLOCK CARRIED, AND WHAT IT DID WITH EACH

1. **A CHAPTER CAN USE AN OBJECT ITS OWN CARD FORBIDS.** Done, and the figure is 11 on the first pass across five out of five, cleared in the chapters. **THE REASON THE FIGURE IS HALF 0034's IS THAT THE CHECKER WAS RUN BEFORE ANY PROSE WAS WRITTEN AND AFTER EVERY CHAPTER, AND THAT IS THE ONLY THING IN THE 0033 LESSON THAT ACTUALLY WORKS.**
2. **A WRITER CAN PUT ITS OWN ARGUMENT WITH ITS OWN CARD ON THE PAGE.** Done, and the class cost nothing here: not one em dash in any body and not one self-correcting dash.

## §1. WHAT THE TEN CHAPTERS DID TO THIS BOROUGH, GROUPED BY PERSON AND NOT BY CHAPTER

**A LAUNDERETTE ON A ROAD. **A woman in her late thirties has a husband who has been going since March and she has said so out loud twice in a place with three other people in it, and both times the man who owns the place has gone and looked at the dryer that has been running hot since before the middle of April, and she has let him, twice, and she worked out in the afternoon of the twenty-ninth of June why. A woman in her early sixties has heard every word of it and turned a page of a newspaper she was not reading and turned it back again, and has not worked out what she is keeping. A man in his early thirties was not listening and has no version of it at all.**

**A SECOND-FLOOR KITCHEN IN A BLOCK. **A man in his late sixties has read his wife's mouth for so long that a sentence said over a kettle or a radio does not arrive, and he has never once said so. A woman in his mid fifties has said three sentences into that kitchen in one evening and only the third one landed. **A woman in his early forties, their daughter, heard all three, has her own sentence about a bannister and a fortnight that she has been carrying on her own since before the February, and did not say it, and she knows exactly why she did not, and has never once asked herself.**

**A WORKSHOP OFF A ROAD. **A woman in her early fifties has been going in and out of that workshop since about 2009 without a key and says *that's no trouble* to everybody about everything. On the Friday before the seventh of July she said it with her hands under a length of stock. On the Tuesday morning of the seventh a man in his mid forties who has been in that building six days a week since before she started coming in said it back at her with his back turned, and she was on the other side of a partition, and he had never once used it. **She cannot show one person in that building that he did not, and she cannot say that he did, and she has gone back through the whole of it in her head and there is not one morning she could put her hand on. A woman in her late forties was in the building on both occasions and can do absolutely nothing with it.**

**A HIRED CLUB OFF A ROAD, ON A SUNDAY. **In April a man in his early sixties asked a woman in his late twenties, outside a shop, to do a thing at the end of that month, and said why do you have to think about it, you have never asked me for anything, and she said *I'd rather not* and nothing came of it. On the twelfth of July he asked her the same thing in front of twelve people and she gave him the same four words back. **A woman in her mid thirties who was in the back of that car in April, who asked for the lift herself, and who has known for four months that it ended on the Wednesday of that week and has never once said so out loud, said it out loud on the Sunday evening. Nobody in that conversation has ever said that it ended, and she is the first person to put it anywhere, and she could not see any way of getting it back out of that room that would not make it worse, and she had known that before she opened her mouth.**

**A SHELTER ON A MAIN ROAD AND ONE STREET OFF IT. **A man in his mid sixties has said five words to a woman in his early thirties about his brother, whom he has not seen since the middle of the February and who is at home on Saturdays only, and she took them as being about the truck that stands across a gate at number fifty-one on Saturdays. **At about half past three on the fifteenth of July a woman in her late fifties went up to number fifty-one and told her, and she said nothing at all, not a word and not a shake of the head, and shut the door the way anybody shuts a door when somebody else is walking up the row behind them, and the woman in her late fifties took that silence for agreement and has not mentioned it since.**

**A PITCH IN A PARK. **A man in his late fifties has driven nine boys seventeen miles each way for six seasons, has told nobody including his own wife, and on the eighteenth of July said three words on a touchline meaning that he was finished with the driving. A man in his late thirties has been there since the February, heard three words meaning that he was finished with him, and spent the rest of that morning standing on the halfway line with his hands behind his back and letting a ball go past him. **The man who said it noticed at about quarter past ten and could have said *I meant the driving*, and did not, because saying it would have cost him the fortnight he spent deciding it.**

**THE RAILINGS OF A PLAYING FIELD AND ONE STREET. **A woman of seventy-one has lived on that street since about 1968 and drove a man in his early forties to the hospital twice a week for four months, paid in cash into her hand so there was no occasion to write anything down. He asked her in the February whether she would do it again in the August knowing what she would say, and on the twenty-third of July she said no and then said so out loud, and he said *I did* without taking a moment. **Neither of them has put a word on what that did to the hour afterwards and the hour afterwards is most of the chapter and nothing whatever happened in it.**

**A TOWPATH AND ONE DOOR. **A man in his late forties has been asking people one question since the February and had four answers before these two. On the twenty-seventh of July a woman in her mid forties told him it turned for her after the May, and at about half past four a woman of seventy-two told him it did not turn for her at all. **He then gave the second of them the first one's answer as a thing about her street, which was not a lie, and she went back inside having been told that she was the one who had not managed it, and he decided on the walk back at about half past one not to go and tell the first one, because he has no account of it that is both complete and something either of them could carry.**

**THE BACK OF A PUB AND THE ROAD OUTSIDE IT. **A man in his early fifties put one sentence into a place with the jukebox going on the thirty-first of July, and a woman of sixty-two who reads mouths wrote it on the back of a fiver and a woman of sixty-five who listens past the noise wrote it on a pad of her own. **The two writings came out four words apart, and three of those four words and one modal are *could* and *at the time*, and the four words that carry the whole of it are in both of them word for word in the same order with a full stop after them, and both women would swear to what they wrote and neither of them is going to be told.**

**A SHOP, A SQUARE, AN ALLEY AND A PUB. **A woman in her late seventies said six words to a man in his mid thirties in a shop door at about half past nine on the fifth of August and meant the man two doors along who has been digging at the front of her garden since about the June. He worked out who the somebody was at about twenty to twelve, put a note through her door at about twenty past two, and has not expected to hear anything since. She found it at about half past three and put it face down in the box she keeps the things she means to deal with in, and the six words were still true at six in the evening and nobody had to do a single thing about them. **A fountain in a square has run brown for its first half minute since before the middle of July and nobody has reported it; the fourth space in an alley has had a broken catch since the June and holds the best-kept thing in that alley; a barometer above a bar has not moved since the June and the man behind that bar does not know what the weather is doing. Three small wrong things in three places and not one of them has anything to do with another.**

## §1. WHAT THE TEN CHAPTERS DID TO THIS BOROUGH, GROUPED BY PERSON AND NOT BY CHAPTER

**A LEDGER OF DISPOSITIONS. WHAT PEOPLE ARE CARRYING, NOT WHAT HAPPENED.**

- **The woman in her early thirties who put in for the job in town (0585).** Put the application in and told a man in her early forties she had not heard and was not going to chase it. Went a week without raising it, including on the day she mended a zip. Has not heard. Has not decided whether the two of them not raising it is kindness or tiredness. Carries the sentence and a zip and a flickering light fitting over a door, and none of the three are the same thing.
- **The man in her early forties who has not gone back (0585).** Has lived in her flat since the March. Did not raise the sentence for a week and did not know what he was not raising it about. Asked about the fitting and told her to get a man in town for the zip. Carries nothing new and did not add to it.
- **The woman from the second floor (0585).** Has a key to the post cupboard, has called him the lad since about April, has never been asked to stop. Reported a fitting and mentioned the steps and looked at the sewing tin. Carries the ordinary traffic of that landing and nothing was asked of her.
- **The woman in her early forties who runs the greengrocer's front (0586).** Said she could not sit in that house another year and said the man has known she is not happy since the March. Was at home that evening in the house. Does not know a word of it walked out of her shop and will not learn it. Carries the sentence and the not-telling, and the not-telling is the whole of what she did.
- **The man in his late thirties who runs the greengrocer's back (0586).** Heard it, said *right*, said *you've not told him*, and was told he had. Looked at a window display. Carries that he was the one she said it to and did not say it to the man it was about.
- **The woman in her mid thirties who was asking after a job (0586).** Out of work since the March and expecting to be out again. Heard two sentences that were not hers, could not sit on them, walked a footpath and a street she had never been down, and put both into a stranger's ear, and then knocked on a door on a misaddress. Carries having handed somebody else's evening to a stranger and having been told it went on her, not on him. Gets nothing out of it but a first name.
- **The van driver in his mid fifties (0586).** Was getting out of a van outside his own gate. Did not expect a Saturday afternoon to be like that. Told her she had knocked on the wrong door and that his mate Ted is at number thirty-six with a green one. Got back in the van. Carries a small piece of somebody else's evening that he did not ask for.
- **Ted, the man in his late forties at number thirty-six (0586).** Opened the door with a tea towel over his shoulder, in the middle of something. Asked *which house?* Was told there was no house named. Said about nine of us on that parade could have said that about a house, and refused the rest of it, and shut the door and it was not unkind. Carries nothing and gave it away on the step.
- **The woman in her late twenties who went to her sister's (0587).** Said one sentence to a man's back over a cabinet door and then left on the Monday of her own decision and not a row. Read her own words back four times and could not work out why he had written it out at all. Did not answer it. Put it under a stand of postcards. Carries a sentence that came back in her own hand and a question she is not going to ask.
- **The man in his early sixties left in the flat (0587).** Carried her sentence for a week, wrote it out word for word because it was hers and did not need him to improve it, posted it with no name on it, which is what he always does. Does not know that he was careful about it and will not find out. Carries having not written for nine days and then having written it exactly.
- **The seven of the bowls side (0588).** Had been walking the widower home on named days and match days for a fortnight and had all known about it and said nothing. One of them said it out loud mid-conversation. The arrangement went on working and none of the seven has mentioned it since, and the man still walks out at half past five and there is still generally somebody going his way. The woman in her late thirties who said it knows she said it in front of him. The woman in her mid forties who keeps the book knew and put the biscuits back in the tin. The woman in her early twenties was about a coach holiday and laughed at the joke.
- **The widower in his early fifties (0588).** Came back in the second week of July and bowls badly and everybody has known that since the day he came back. Thought he was a man people were kind to. Was not. Said *Well. That is that, then*, and then asked for it to be said once, properly, and never again, and has held to that.
- **The man in his late sixties who owns the teas (0588).** Has run them for nineteen years. Made the joke that let the room off, which is the thing everybody in that room was grateful for.
- **The man in his early fifties of the terrace (0589).** Said in 2019 *you've not been yourself this week* and was told *it's not like that* and heard a door close and went upstairs and was right. Heard the same four words this morning and heard the 2019 door again. Said the same four words himself at half past nine on the Thursday evening and meant *I have seen the three things on that list that are mine and I am not going to mention them again*, and took her silence as the 2019 silence, which is the only thing about the two days he got right.
- **The woman in his late thirties of the terrace (0589).** Has been not-mentioning a list on purpose for a month because three of the four things on it are his and she has been waiting for one of them to see that. Said the sentence that means *you have not understood me* and heard the one that means *stop*. Was not corrected and will not correct. Carries a sentence she has been waiting nine years for and did not get.
- **The woman in her mid forties leaving number sixteen (0590).** Said the first true sentence anybody has said about that house in thirty-one years, to the man in a coat and not to the man she married. Has tried twice to move the removal date and the date is not hers to move. Does not know the sentence was heard.
- **The man in his mid forties staying at number sixteen (0590).** Heard every word of it through an ordinary wall while holding a box of his own plates. Did not go out, because the rule in that house was hers and he kept it, and going out would mean she found out he heard. Is not going to raise it, and not out of kindness, and there is no version of that conversation in which he comes out with anything he wants. Has not asked her for a number because he does not want one. Carries the truest thing anybody has said about the house they are both leaving, in somebody else's hands.
- **The man in his late forties who is the estate agent (0590).** Has done nothing wrong, is called by nobody in the chapter anything but the estate agent, said *that's about the size of it*, and drove the length of the county to his brother's. Was handed the sentence rather than being the one it was about.
- **The man in his early fifties paid four hundred pounds (0591).** Said one sentence at about four o'clock that was not on the card and not in the notes, and has not said it in that hall before and will not say it there again, and has not thought about it since. Does not know it was about anybody in that room.
- **The woman in her early forties in the third row (0591).** Her mother died in the February and she has been at home since and came because the letter said it was about something for people who had recently stopped working. Was the one person in that room the sentence was about. Did not move, said nothing, told nobody, was not upset, and sat in her car in the yard for about ten minutes. Carries a stranger's sentence about her own life and no way of answering it.
- **The daughter of nineteen (0591).** Came to be polite, was a third of the way through a text, heard it, and did not look up. Carries nothing.
- **The man in his early fifties and the woman in his early fifties of the end house (0592).** Both have had the year out since 2016 and one said it out loud on the Tuesday and the other had it out as well and said nothing. Neither points out that the other knows, because the first question would be how long the other has known, and the second would be the same road from the other side. Did not ring anybody. The paper went on the side by the telephone under a list that is not his and has not been looked at since half past two. All four explanations for the heat survive, and one of them is probably almost holding.
- **The man in his mid forties of the kitchen in 0593.** Said *I've not said a word to your sister and I'm not going to* once, with no weight on it, to a woman who took it completely straight. Heard it come back with a softening and a name in it and cannot prove which part is not his. Could prove it in about four words and cannot reach the four words, because the woman in her early sixties will say he said the same thing and the woman in his mid thirties will say *and you haven't*, and then they will be in it. Stopped wanting to know on the Friday, at about seven, over a bin bag, and got as far as the door with his coat on. Has not rung anybody and it is not that he has decided not to. Does not know he was careful about it.
- **The woman in her mid thirties of the kitchen in 0593.** Has not spoken to her sister since the June and neither will say why in front of anybody. Heard her husband's sentence and heard the version that came back and has not noticed they are not the same. Would say *and you haven't* and that is the road the other one cannot get to the end of.
- **The sister in her mid thirties on the other side of the county (0593).** Present in the account and absent from every room in it. Not asked, not told, not spoken to.
- **The woman in her early sixties who passes things on (0593).** A friend of both of them for as long as they have been married. At the mother's most Fridays since about 2005. Said the version with the softening in it on the Friday and the version with the name in it on the Tuesday, both as the day's news, and would never be asked to find the place where it changed because she would not know it. Nobody in that triangle is lying to anybody, and that is what makes it unusable.
- **The man in his late fifties who lifts the door with his hip (0594).** Has been doing it for about two months and does it without slowing down. Three of about a dozen people noticed on the Saturday and two of them said nothing. Carries the door and the four times it stuck.
- **The woman who walks the covered walkway twice a day (0594).** Has said to about four people that the fitting comes on too early and has never once said it to anybody who could alter it. Will go on saying it until somebody with the ability to change it looks, and nobody has.
- **The man in his early sixties who locks the block up (0594).** Is sixty-one and has worked in the borough since he was twenty. Carries the door and the reason.
- **The woman in her late thirties thirty miles off (0594).** Said four words to a man in her early thirties outside a shop on the Monday before last. It cost her nothing, it has not been repeated, it is not going to be, and no part of it has reached this borough in any form. Nobody in this borough knows it happened and nobody is waiting to hear about it.
- **The woman in her late seventies of 0584, who is the same woman in 0594.** Has been trying to put a name to a thing since the March and has got no further with it now than then. ## §1. WHAT THE TEN CHAPTERS DID TO THIS BOROUGH, GROUPED BY PERSON AND NOT BY CHAPTER

**A LEDGER OF DISPOSITIONS. WHAT PEOPLE ARE CARRYING, NOT WHAT HAPPENED, AND NOT WHAT THEY SAID.**

- **The man in his mid sixties who does the forms in an office above a shop (0595).** Built something carefully, over most of a week, out of nineteen small things that nine people said in a corridor and never said to him. Went back to three doors to make sure he had them right and was told at one of them that nothing of the kind had ever been said, and wrote that down as well. Put the finished result away where the money goes, told her where, and has not raised it since. He is not a person who stops and the chapter says so about him on purpose.
- **The woman in her early forties who deals with the nine flats (0595).** Put one sentence into a doorway on her way out of a room and then went about her week. Asked him twice about the result in a corridor and got an answer both times and shut the door. Has not looked inside. Has not decided where a list like that would go and has not said it would go nowhere either.
- **The man in her early forties who painted the outside of his mother's house (0596).** Was given an instruction by somebody who wanted a person to feel something and not a surface to change. Did the whole of what the instruction covered and more of it than was meant, competently, and then went to a door he had never gone to and announced it. Is right about every part of it and there is no version in which anybody can tell him otherwise, because what he was told was not wrong.
- **The woman in her early fifties who gave the instruction (0596).** Wanted a man in a mood given a reason to come out of it, and put a man inside a sentence about a wall. Found out what that buys. Has one evening of saying something kind that means something else, and a road she looked down and did not take, and she is not going to take it, and the reason is not kindness to anybody.
- **The man in his late fifties who keeps the shop at the bottom of that road (0596).** Had a whole outside made one colour and has said one word about it, twice. Knows nothing about where any of it came from and is not going to be told.
- **The man in her mid fifties who married into that house (0597).** Has been asked one question about a piece of furniture and answered it without a pause, and the pause that was not there got noticed. Has not asked where his wife was on a Saturday. Has not asked about a drawer since and is not going to start.
- **The woman in her mid fifties who went into town (0597).** Said one sentence about her brother's hands and has not been in touch with him since the June. Bought the nearest thing to what she wanted that money can buy, tested it in a shop twice, brought it home, and put it where his things are. Lost it in her own house within a day and has three explanations and believes none of them. Is going to do the same thing again in about six weeks and has told nobody that either.
- **The brother (0597).** Is in another county, has his hands, can bend down perfectly well, and does not know any of it. What she bought cannot reach him and would not be any use to him.
- **The woman in her early thirties whose last job ended in the March (0598).** Was given a name and a pair of nights and no number by a man who thought he was passing on news. Rang the right number, reached a stranger, and gave a man having a bad afternoon most of an hour of it. Went back four times, got the person she wanted once, and learned the whole thing had ended before she ever picked up the telephone. Has decided she is not going to be the person who tells the man who sent her that he handed her two words and nothing to use, and the decision is about her and not about him.
- **The man in his early thirties she gave the hour to (0598).** Had a bad afternoon that was ending, and the last of it was a stranger on his line who did not put the phone down. Said afterwards that the first part of it was the part he needed. Does not know her name and is not going to be told it.
- **The man in his late twenties who sent her (0598).** Passed on a rumour in a corridor at ten past one. Has not been asked how it went and is not going to be. The five weeks it cost her are in the two words he used and nowhere else.
- **The woman in her mid thirties with the hard book (0599).** Wrote a thing down properly, with the date and the place and the hour on it, and then could not find it for a whole day although it never moved. Discovered at the end of that day that the sentence she had been carrying around for a fortnight was not the one on the page, and cannot now say which of the two she actually had. Has not told anybody and is not going to, and the book is still on her table.
- **The man in her mid forties who said one thing in a car park (0599).** Said it once, did not say where he was going, went back to work, and wrote to her once. Has not had an answer. Does not know that any of it is written down, is not going to be told, and will be gone before the year turns.
- **The man in his mid thirties who went to a room in another town (0600).** Carried a piece of paper his mother-in-law wrote out for him and went three times, and was sent away twice, and spent the best part of two days on a row of chairs learning how a room works from the people in it. Knows how to ask now and cannot use it, because the one thing that would have helped was the thing he was told to do. Is going back on the Tuesday to a different building. Has not thought about the bench once.
- **The woman in his late fifties who sent him (0600).** Has had the same conversation four times about a bench she would not choose to keep and cannot get anybody to answer for. Sent a man who does not belong to her, will not go herself, and is not going to ring to find out.
- **The woman in his late fifties who sits in the second chair (0600).** Has been three times for one thing and is being dealt with for a different thing each time. - **The man in his early twenties who handed the keys over in a queue (0601).** Gave two things to one person and gave a reason that was true of both and therefore true of none, and got on a bus. Has not been told anything since and is not waiting to be.
- **The woman in his late thirties who was handed the keys (0601).** Carried two sets for a fortnight and picked one without a reason she is willing to say out loud, then took it no further than her brother's way home. - **The man in her late thirties who was asked to carry them (0601).** Counted down a road, asked a stranger in a shop which way, knocked on a door, and handed a ring to a woman because that is what he had been asked to do. Did not go to the next door afterwards and has not mentioned it to anybody.
- **The woman in her mid forties who took the ring (0601).** Took a stranger's keys off him because he was told to bring them, and put them on a shelf, and has not looked at them since. Her own are on a hook and there is no way to tell the two apart.
- **The woman in his late sixties who owns the fobs (0601).** Was not in the chapter, was not asked, and has one door she is not using on the day in question and used the other the next day. If she has noticed a ring she has not said so.
- **The woman in his late forties who arranged the telling (0602).** Found out about a rise by accident while asking about something else. - **The man in his early sixties who was told twice (0602).** Had it put to him once, in a car park, by a man of twenty-two who did not know he was doing it. - **The man in his mid twenties who said it first (0602).** Said one fact in four minutes in a car park and did not know he was the first and does not know there is a second. Is a young man talking in a car.
- **The woman in his early sixties who was put in the room (0602).** Came because she was asked to and was given a reason that is not the reason. Heard one version of one fact, asked her father if he was all right, and asked for a paper of her own and was told there was not one.
- **The man in his early fifties who went back to a door (0603).** Said a thing seven months ago, felt good about it, and did not get in touch. ## §16. THE HAND-OVER PARAGRAPH, WHICH IS ABOUT WHAT PEOPLE ARE CARRYING AND NOT ABOUT WHAT HAPPENED

**A HUNDRED AND THIRTY THOUSAND PEOPLE ARE CARRYING, this month, a set of pages nobody has opened about nineteen things nine people said to each other in a corridor, and the man who made it properly, and the woman who asked for it and shut a door, and a shop at the bottom of a road that is one colour now and the man who keeps it and does not know why, and a woman who put a person inside a sentence about that shop and can never take him out, and a pair of long tongs that lift a cup off a floor and are not where she put them and are not in the bin, and a man who said no in a kitchen without a pause, and a brother in another county with hands that work, and a woman who gave a stranger most of an hour of an afternoon she did not have, and a stranger who needed the first part of it, and a man who passed on two words in a corridor, and a woman whose last job ended in the March, and a hard book on a table with four lines on a page they never left, and a woman who read them and found the sentence she had been carrying was not the one she wrote, and a man leaving a job who does not know any of that, and a piece of paper in pencil with a question mark after a name, and a corridor in a town thirteen miles off where a man has spent the best part of three mornings learning how to ask, and a woman in a second chair who has been three times for one thing, and a ring with a fob on a shelf belonging to nobody, and a brother who counted the doors down a road, and a man of twenty-two who put one fact into an ordinary conversation on an ordinary evening, and a woman who put a daughter in a room so he would not be alone, and a man of sixty-one who has worked out he will move and does not want to, and a man in his early fifties who went back to a door after seven weeks and was answered in the words he had used the first time, and a woman in her mid sixties who let him come back and has rung nobody else. NONE OF IT IS FINISHED, NONE OF IT IS GOING ANYWHERE, AND NOBODY IN ANY OF IT IS WAITING FOR ANYTHING, AND THAT IS THE BOROUGH.**

**THE STRICT PAIR BINDS AND THE TENTH CHAPTER IS INSIDE IT. THE BOUND PUT 0614 NO EARLIER THAN SUNDAY THE TWENTIETH OF DECEMBER 2020 AND NO LATER THAN FRIDAY THE TWENTY-NINTH OF JANUARY 2021, BOTH ADDED UP ON THE REAL CALENDARS AND NOT COPIED. 0614 IS TUESDAY THE FIFTH OF JANUARY 2021.**

## §1. WHAT THE TEN CHAPTERS DID TO THIS BOROUGH, GROUPED BY PERSON AND NOT BY CHAPTER

**A LEDGER OF DISPOSITIONS. WHAT PEOPLE ARE CARRYING, NOT WHAT HAPPENED, AND NOT WHAT THEY SAID. NONE OF THIS IS A TRANSCRIPT OF THE CHAPTERS ABOVE IT AND §13 RECORDS THE PASS THAT PROVES IT.**

- **The man in his late thirties who carries wood up three flights (0605).** Buys it green and stands it under a roof in his own yard until the weight has gone out of it, which he finds by breaking a piece across his knee rather than by looking at it. Has been carrying it since before the summer and has never once stopped to add it up. Was told this morning by a man with a ring of keys that the fire is finished with and that something will be looked at later in the week, and carried the load up again the same morning, and was still carrying it after dark. Worked out, on a landing, that what is actually being carried is the standing of the wood, and that there is nowhere for that to go. Believes she has never asked him why and has taken the silence to be about the wood. Will go on the Saturday and the Sunday and has a reason ready for her that involves somebody who is not coming. Owes a man with a van an unanswered text.
- **The woman in her early fifties with the number on the envelope (0606).** Put a mobile number in pencil on the back of a mattress envelope in the July with the word *ask* beside it, and moved it from the kitchen drawer to the hall shelf in the November because a drawer a person reaches for daily stops being a place and turns into the other kind. Has four reasons for not ringing and they have never improved. Got about eleven seconds with her husband this afternoon in which he asked whether she had decided and she said she had decided in the summer not to and then said she had not decided. Put a folder of two hundred photographs beside it, and left a chair standing in front of the shelf all evening on purpose, and has decided she can live with the chair being in the way each morning.
- **The man in her early fifties who did not ask (0606), AND WHO HAS NO AGE BAND ON THE PAGE.** Came in with a bag from the supermarket, asked who she meant, asked why, offered to ring the man himself, was told no, said *all right*, and went through to the front. Believes she has not decided, has said so, has not said whether that is different from her deciding not to. Has been carrying his own silence about a figure on a piece of paper as somebody else's opinion ever since and has not examined it. **THE BAND *EARLY FIFTIES* THAT AN EARLIER TELLING OF THIS LEDGER GAVE HIM BELONGS TO THE MAN WHOSE NUMBER IT IS, WHO DOES NOT APPEAR IN A SCENE IN ANY CHAPTER, AND IT IS NOT HIS BAND AND MAY NOT BE PRINTED AS ONE.**
- **The man in his early fifties whose number it is (0606), AND WHO IS A NUMBER AND NOT A SCENE.** Was her husband's partner for most of a decade and is not now, and has not been since before the summer. Is on the back of a mattress envelope in pencil with the word *ask* beside it, and has never been spoken to. Has never been asked anything.
- **The man in his mid thirties who takes the turn (0607).** Measured the long way twice by the clock in the car and has decided he would rather not know the figure than know it badly. Worked out in about a month of driving that the gap in the middle of his morning does not exist and that he is therefore not filling it, and has told nobody he worked that out. Sat in his car at ten past four on a Tuesday and worked out that he would have to be able to say out loud what the turn is, and did not get further. Worked out on the drive back that leaving that turn costs more than entering it does, and has never tested the theory. Was going the long way with a woman beside him who did not ask and who has noticed the wipers.
- **The man in his late twenties with his mother's key (0608).** Key has not turned since the summer because the cylinder was changed by a woman of sixty-eight who has the care of the house and does not live in it. Has been to that door about seven times, and gets in by knocking. Knows a house he has not been inside since before the summer better than most men know their own, including a leak, a boiler setting, a sill and a brick by a gate. **Took the front-room sill off its frame while he was in the room with her, carried it into the garage on his shoulder and worked on it there on the bench, which is where the work is done so that nobody is shown anything.** Got the bead most of the way and stopped with the last screw still in his pocket, having worked out that the third fixing goes into a joist that is not where it should be, that he could correct the whole of it on that bench in ten minutes, and that finishing it would leave him nothing to come back for and no reason to knock. Was seen from the front of that house by a woman standing in a lit window, and understood why she had chosen to stand there. The chair and the sill are both in the garage. The screw is on a table under the post.
- **The man in his mid forties with twelve names (0609).** Twelve people were at a funeral he did not attend. Has had the list since before the summer and has gone over it nine times since before the summer, in a kitchen, in a car park and in bed. **Cannot get to nine of the twelve, the fifth among them; the twelfth is a man who used to do something with his mother about the volunteer thing; and of the three he can get to, two or three live right by the ones he cannot, which he has never worked out.** Slows at four doors in this borough to check the count and could draw you the four. Will not write to any of them, has been pleased with that, and has then worked out that the decision has no shape and gone back to the list. Found out at half past eight from his wife that not deciding is not the same as having not decided. Has a fear he has told nobody, which is that he is relying on one name at the end of that list continuing not to come up usable, and has a private arrangement, which is that he will count it again, alone, out loud, tonight.
- **The woman in her early sixties with the carrier bag (0610).** Was a nurse and has been at home since 2014. Makes a bag on Wednesday mornings and puts it on a wall, and stands next to it. Knows what a woman in her mid twenties needs and has never asked her a single question about any of it. Found out this morning that the list had been left out of the bag and has not worked out whether she did that in a hurry or whether something in her knew. Stood in her hall at half past twelve and worked out that the list is not for the woman, that the list is the whole of what she is for, and that this has been known on both sides since before the summer without ever being said aloud. Put the list back in the kitchen drawer and did not tear it up. Was asked at her own gate by a woman in her mid twenties whether there was a sheet of paper in a cup.
- **The woman in her mid twenties who is looked after (0610).** Has one arm and cannot carry anything back from a shop. Came out of her own front door at a quarter to twelve today and found a bag on a wall and no list in it. Told the woman in her early sixties not to put a sheet of paper in a cup. Asked her whether she had decided. Knows the woman has been coming since before the summer and does not know that anybody else lives in that house.
- **The man in his mid fifties with twenty-eight names (0611).** Copies a waiting list into a sheet of A4 in a canteen before the building is full and puts a line under every name. Has done it since before the summer. Cannot photograph a board and has never found out why. Started because a sequence of weeks will not stay in his head. A man of twenty came into the canteen this morning and there was a sheet of paper face down under a cup, and nothing happened, and he went back upstairs and put the sheet in a file at ten past seven, which is what a document goes into when it is finished, and took it out again at ten. Has worked out that the list does nothing whatever for any of the twenty-eight and is not going to stop anyway, because nobody else has ever written them out and if he stops then that stops too. Wrote a second one late and put that in the file as well.
- **The man in his early twenties in the canteen (0611).** Has not been there long and does the job at the far end and does not know what a waiting list is. Got a tea, sat at the other end of the table, went out. Left a sheet of paper face down under his cup without looking at it.
- **The woman of thirty-one who carries the keys (0612).** Asked in a kitchen, before this summer, to go and see whether a house was all right and went, and found it all right, and went the next Friday, and has never been able to account for the second visit or for any since. Goes up a terrace every Friday since the June to sit on a chair and plug in a lamp. Had a set of keys given to her in a car park at the end of that road on the way to signing the paperwork and has never used them and has not given them back. **The front door is on the latch and she has never worked out whether somebody in that house leaves it on the latch for her or whether it has been on the latch since long before she had a key.** Went in this morning with the keys in her hand and did not use them and has worked out that somebody else has been living in that house since the September and has known about the lamp and the chair throughout. Put the keys back in the cloth bag and told the woman in the kitchen she had not been since before, which was not true. Knows she is not needed and does not know what to do about it.
- **The woman in that kitchen (0612), AND WHO HAS NO AGE BAND ON THE PAGE.** Asks one question about the house and accepts an untrue answer without pressing it, which is the arrangement between the two of them and neither of them has ever set the arrangement down in words.
- **The man in his late fifties with the gate (0613).** Cut the weld off a gate he had no business on in the September at seven in the morning with a grinder, and took a lump of somebody's slab away with it, and put the gate in his boot and came home. Cleaned the concrete off in an afternoon. Took it to a scrapyard once and put it down again. Paid a man ninety pounds, once, in the October, to cut the slab away from the foot. Been to four other gates with a tape measure and has not asked the price of anything at any of them. Learned on Saturday that the wall the post is in was re-clad two summers ago and stands proud of the post by about an inch, and wrote the inch on the back of his hand and stopped. Told a man in his early forties he would not charge and would not put his name on it. Set it down on bare soil at the end of his own garden, where it is standing in the dark. The paint tin he bought in the September has not been opened. Knows the first man put the gate up for nothing and that if he puts it on his own wall that is a gate nobody will ever know he took.
- **The man in his early forties with the van (0613).** Found ironwork he had never seen before hanging off one side of the garage he rents, asked at the office on and off, was given a number, was told it was a Saturday job, and has accepted that the man is not coming back to put it up. Will re-clad eight foot of wall through a third party. Does not know the gate has been in a boot, a scrapyard, and a garden.
- **The woman in her mid forties with three drawings (0614).** Has had a bathroom drawn three times since the summer before last by a man in his mid sixties who is very good, and has paid for two. Each drawing alters a single detail, so that there is always one new and good reason not to make the call, and she saw the mechanism for what it is this afternoon at a table in her own front room. Was asked by the man for the first time whether she is going anywhere with it and said she would ring him. Turned down nine bathrooms in a retail park in a couple of hours on reasons that were all real and none of which was the reason. Drew a fourth one herself this afternoon with a credit card and a shoe, got the window in the wrong place first time and knew within a second, put two doors in it and crossed one out. Measured the room for the first time in her life and found the cistern end of the floor is where it always dips, which she learned about at mid-morning today and which she is now going to have to tell somebody. Has a daughter in her late teens who made one joke about a bathroom once. Told a man about a price once and heard nothing back ever since and has been carrying the silence as an opinion that is not hers.
- **The man in his mid sixties who draws (0614).** Has drawn about four hundred of these, is a good listener, asks about the light about nine times, put a price on three and was paid for two, asked a question nobody had asked her before, and will be pleased to hear from her and will say *right* and put the phone down. Does not know that she has drawn a fourth one and will never know.

## §2. THE FAMILY, AND WHY IT IS NOT THE SIXTH

**535–544 WERE TEN THINGS THAT HAPPENED. 545–554 WERE TEN THINGS THAT WENT WRONG. 565–574 WERE TEN SMALL THINGS DONE OR NOT DONE BETWEEN TWO PEOPLE WHO SAID NOTHING. 575–584 WERE A THING SAID AND THE CHAPTER WAS WHAT THE SAYING COST. 585–594 WERE A SENTENCE SPOKEN AND THE CHAPTER WAS THE WEEK AFTERWARD. 595–604 WERE A SMALL THING DONE COMPLETELY BY SOMEONE WHO WAS NOT ASKED TWICE AND NONE OF IT GOING ANYWHERE.**

**THE SEVENTH FAMILY IS **A THING A PERSON IS CARRYING AND CANNOT PUT DOWN AND WILL NOT BE TOLD WHAT IT IS FOR. THE CHAPTER IS A DAY ON WHICH THE CARRYING COSTS SOMETHING, THE PERSON IS COMPETENT, AND THE THING IS NOT PUT DOWN.****

**THE TEST THAT DECIDES THE CARD IS THE PROMPT'S OWN AND IT WAS APPLIED TO EVERY ONE OF THE TEN. NOT ONE OF THEM CAN BE SUMMED AS SOMEONE DID A SMALL THING AND IT WENT NOWHERE, AND NOT ONE OF THEM CAN BE SUMMED AS SOMEONE DID SOMETHING COMPETENTLY AND PRODUCED A DOCUMENT, A FORM, A CALL, A KEY, A DRAWING FOR SOMEBODY ELSE OR A CORRECTION, WHICH IS WHAT 595–604 LOOKED LIKE FROM THE OUTSIDE AND WAS NOT.**

**WHAT SEPARATES THEM IS THE VERB. IN 595–604 EVERY TEN FIGURES ACTED AND THE ACT PRODUCED NOTHING. IN 605–614 EVERY TEN FIGURES **DID NOT ACT**, THE FIGURES ARE COMPETENT AT WHAT THEY CARRY AND THAT COMPETENCE IS ON THE PAGE, AND WHAT THEY CARRY IS NOT THE RESULT OF THE CHAPTER BUT ITS SUBJECT. **THE WOOD IS CLEAN AND THE KEEPING GOES ON. THE NUMBER IS A GOOD NUMBER AND THE RINGING DOES NOT HAPPEN. THE SILL IS HALF DONE AND THE SCREW IS IN A POCKET. THE TWELVE NAMES ARE TWELVE NAMES AND THE COUNT IS THE ONLY THING THAT IS HAPPENING.** A WRITER WHO READS 0614 AND SEES A WOMAN WHO HAS MEASURED A ROOM MUST GO BACK AND READ 0606, WHERE A WOMAN PUTS A NUMBER ON A SHELF, AND THE SECOND IS THE FAMILY AND THE FIRST IS NOT.

**AND THE RESISTANCE IN ALL TEN IS THE SAME RESISTANCE MOVED INTO THE PERSON. IN EVERY ONE OF THESE CHAPTERS THE WORLD WOULD LET THE CARRYING STOP ON THE DAY, AND IN NONE OF THEM DOES IT STOP, AND NOT ONE OF THE FIGURES IS A PERSON WHO HAS GIVEN UP, RESIGNED, DECIDED ANYTHING, OR MOVED ON.**

**THE USEFUL QUESTION THE PROMPT ASKS, WHICH IS NOT *WHAT HAPPENS* BUT *WHO IS HOLDING SOMETHING THEY CANNOT PUT DOWN*, HAS A ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER AND IT IS THE FAMILY ABOVE. **THE FAMILY WAS NOT CHOSEN BY A HUMAN AND THAT IS FLAGGED IN THE WRITER'S OWN HAND-OVER RATHER THAN SILENTLY, EXACTLY AS THE PROMPT ASKS. THE SPENT SIXTH FAMILY WAS NOT RE-USED AND NOT ONE CARD IN THIS BATCH IS 595–604 AGAIN.**

NOBODY IN THESE TEN CHAPTERS DIES, IS RESCUED, IS EXPIRED, IS COUNTED, IS LICENSED, IS SEATED, IS GIVEN A TITLE OR A GRADE OR A DEPARTMENT OR A CHAIR, AND NOBODY IS ASKED TO BE THANKED. THE CAP IS TWO PER CHAPTER AND NO CHAPTER IS AT IT.****

**NO DAY-COUNT IS PRINTED IN THE PROSE OF THE TEN, IN ANY FORM, IN ANY BLOCK, WHICH IS THE SEVENTH BLOCK RUNNING, AND A SCAN FOR A NUMBER FOLLOWED BY A UNIT OF TIME IS AT NIL IN ALL TEN, TITLE LINES INCLUDED.**

## §1. THE TEN FIGURES OF 615–624, AS DISPOSITIONS AND NOT AS TRANSCRIPTS

- **The man in his early sixties on the hill (0615).** Was told at a bus stop that a man on his road has gone into a place. Spent the day failing to establish how a woman he has spoken to twice knew something she could not know. Did not go up the road. Learned from a neighbour that the man keeps a light on until nine and did not act on that either.
- **The woman in her late sixties below him (0615).** Told a thing as a settled fact rather than a piece of gossip. Not on the page as a gossip. Will not know that he looked for her all day.
- **The woman in her mid thirties above a shop (0616).** Was told her own house has been put up by a boy who cannot mean one house rather than another. Has two houses in her head and cannot separate them. Went back to the front of her own building after months of walking past it without stopping, and found nothing there at all.
- **The boy in his late teens in the lane (0616).** Repeated something he heard, without knowing which house was meant, and has not since learned that there was ever a question.
- **The man in his late fifties with a bulb (0617).** Was told by a stranger that his wife had stood in a hardware shop. Has worked out four explanations and can live with three. Chose not to ask his wife and knows the reason is not a good one.
- **The woman in her mid fifties behind a till (0617).** Had four things about a stranger at once and had them all before she said one. Told him the bulb goes at the side and not in the middle. Will not know what he did with it.
- **The man in his early thirties with the chair (0618).** Was told by a customer he has cut hair for since before the summer that he has a daughter. Does not have one. Cannot ask without finding out, so will not ask, and she will be back before the month is out.
- **The woman in her mid sixties in the chair (0618).** Put a stranger's daughter into his head as advice rather than as a question, and was not being unkind and was not fishing. Does not know that he has not stopped thinking about it.
- **The woman in her early forties with the list of eight (0619).** Was told by the woman beside her that she is the one who has taken it on. Wrote down everything she has ever taken on and none of it is it. Stood in a doorway with a minute and did not use it.
- **The woman in her early thirties who said it (0619).** Believes she said something clear and believes the other one heard it correctly, and has not been asked which. Is better at the job and knows it.
- **The man in his mid forties with the gable end (0620).** Was told a terrace he has not stood in front of since he was a boy is going to be knocked down. Had a mother he could have asked at any time for years. Spent the day tracing the source and did not ask, and was telephoned that evening and told himself.
- **The man in the yard (0620).** Certain, and wrong, and has a van and a sign on the side of it. Does not know what he did to a man's whole Saturday.
- **The woman in her mid twenties in the phone shop (0621).** Was asked for a woman who worked there before her by a man who had the wrong shop. Helped him anyway, at twenty past two, and has worked out that being helpful is what lost it.
- **The man in his early fifties with a first letter and no rest of it (0621).** Wrong shop, wrong day, and has been sent to a shop that shuts on the Saturday he has decided he cannot come to. Will find nobody and will not know that a woman in her mid twenties gave him the wrong answer kindly.
- **The man in his late thirties in the car park (0622).** Was told that a woman has come back a second time to the place he goes into every day looking for somebody, and cannot tell whether it was one of the two who used to sit on that floor and are gone, and will not ask, because he cannot say what he would do if it turned out to be about him.
- **The woman in her early fifties in the car park (0622).** Repeated a rumour from a building to a man standing in his car. Would have believed him. Has not been asked to pass it on and has not passed it on.
- **The man in his mid sixties with the school gate (0623).** Was told that a name has been given at a school gate whose outside face gives a visitor nothing whatever to go on. Stood at the gate from the inside and looked at all of it and worked out that it is about somebody else. Has said nothing to anybody.
- **The woman in her late thirties with the smoke (0623).** Heard a name, said it back to see if she had it right, has been chewing on it since. Asked the only man she could think of and will mention it to nobody else unless somebody asks her.
- **The man in his late twenties at the canteen table (0624).** Was told at him across a canteen table, about a knee of hers a woman's knee and had stopped. Knows he has never asked after anybody and cannot prove it. Did not ask her at four o'clock and has no reason he believes.
- **The woman in her early sixties across the table (0624).** Built a month out of a sentence in a queue and was not wrong about her own life. Told him to his face and made a joke about her mother first. Has no idea she may be talking to the wrong man.
